as \mathbf Q-vector spaces. The condition n>1 is used so that the term K_{n-1}(Z) in the localization sequence is a well-defined higher K-group at the position needed; the argument does not otherwise depend on the finiteness of k. \square

lemma_51.statement: Let U be a noetherian scheme, let Z be a regular closed subscheme of U, and let V = U \setminus Z. Let n > 0. If K_n(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0 and K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0, then K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.
lemma_51.proof:
Proof. We use the Quillen localization theorem for K-theory of schemes in the standard noetherian form: if U is a noetherian scheme and Z is a regular closed subscheme of U, with V=U\setminus Z, then K(Z)\to K(U)\to K(V) is a homotopy fiber sequence. Equivalently, for every m\ge 0 there is a long exact sequence \cdots\to K_m(Z)\to K_m(U)\to K_m(V)\to K_{m-1}(Z)\to\cdots. The hypotheses of the present lemma are exactly those required for this theorem: U is noetherian by assumption, Z is a regular closed subscheme, and V is the open complement (hence noetherian). Therefore, for the given n>0, the segment K_n(Z)\to K_n(U)\to K_n(V) is exact at K_n(U), i.e. \operatorname{im}(K_n(Z)\to K_n(U))=\ker(K_n(U)\to K_n(V)).

The abelian group \mathbf{Q} is flat over \mathbf{Z}. Indeed, \mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{Z}[1/(\mathbf{Z}\setminus\{0\})] is a filtered colimit of copies of \mathbf{Z}; each copy is free, hence flat, and filtered colimits of flat modules are flat. Consequently, tensoring the exact segment with \mathbf{Q} preserves exactness, so

K_n(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}\to K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}\to K_n(V)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}

is exact at the middle term.

By hypothesis, K_n(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0 and K_n(V)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0. Exactness at the middle term then gives

\ker\big(K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}\to 0\big)=\operatorname{im}\big(0\to K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}\big)=0.

But the kernel of the unique map from an abelian group to 0 is the whole group. Hence K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0.

The degenerate cases are consistent with the same argument. If Z=\emptyset, then V=U and the hypothesis K_n(V)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0 is exactly the desired conclusion. If V=\emptyset, then Z=U and the hypothesis K_n(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0 is exactly the desired conclusion. If U=\emptyset, all three K-groups are zero. This completes the proof.

lemma_54.statement: Let U be a regular noetherian scheme, let Z be a regular closed subscheme of U, let V=U\setminus Z, and let n>1. Then the sequence K_n(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(V)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} induced by the inclusion and restriction maps is exact.
lemma_54.proof: Proof. We use Quillen's localization theorem: if X is a regular noetherian scheme, Z_0 is a regular closed subscheme of X, and W = X \setminus Z_0, then for every integer m \ge 1 there is a long exact sequence of abelian groups \cdots \to K_m(Z_0) \to K_m(X) \to K_m(W) \to K_{m-1}(Z_0) \to K_{m-1}(X) \to \cdots, in which the first map is induced by the closed immersion Z_0 \hookrightarrow X, the second by the open immersion W \hookrightarrow X, and the third is the connecting homomorphism. Apply this theorem with X = U, Z_0 = Z, and W = V. The hypotheses are satisfied exactly as stated: U is regular noetherian by assumption, and Z is a regular closed subscheme of U by assumption. Since n > 1, we have n \ge 2, so the case m = n is allowed. Therefore we obtain an exact sequence K_n(Z) \to K_n(U) \to K_n(V) \to K_{n-1}(Z) \to K_{n-1}(U), with the first map induced by the inclusion Z \hookrightarrow U and the second by the restriction/open immersion V \hookrightarrow U. If Z is empty or equal to U, the same conclusion is immediate from K_*(\varnothing)=0 and the identity map; the theorem also covers these degenerate cases. Next we tensor with \mathbf{Q}. The abelian group \mathbf{Q} is flat over \mathbf{Z}: indeed \mathbf{Q} = S^{-1}\mathbf{Z} with S = \mathbf{Z} \setminus \{0\}, and for any injective homomorphism f:A\to B of \mathbf{Z}-modules, the map S^{-1}f:S^{-1}A\to S^{-1}B is injective, because if s^{-1}a maps to 0, then t f(a)=0 for some t\in S, and injectivity of f gives t a=0, hence s^{-1}a=0. Thus -\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} is an exact functor on \mathbf{Z}-modules. Applying it to the exact sequence above yields an exact sequence (K_n(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}) \to (K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}) \to (K_n(V)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}) \to (K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}) \to (K_{n-1}(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}). The maps in this tensored sequence are precisely the original inclusion and restriction maps tensored with the identity on \mathbf{Q}. Exactness of a long exact sequence at its interior terms gives \operatorname{im}(K_n(Z)\otimes\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf{Q}) = \ker(K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(V)\otimes\mathbf{Q}) and \operatorname{im}(K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(V)\otimes\mathbf{Q}) = \ker(K_n(V)\otimes\mathbf{Q} \to K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes\mathbf{Q}). This is exactly the required exactness of the four-term sequence. No appeal to finite type or to external context is needed; the noetherian hypothesis on U is part of the statement and is used directly in Quillen's theorem. Q.E.D.

lemma_55.statement: Let k be a finite field, let C be a smooth projective curve over k, let p be a closed point of C, and let n > 1. Then K_n(C)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} is isomorphic to K_n(C\setminus\{p\})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} as \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces.
lemma_55.proof:
We prove that K_n(C)⊗_Z Q ≅ K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q as Q-vector spaces.

Step 1: Verify the hypotheses of lemma_54.
Let U = C, Z = {p} (viewed as a closed subscheme of C), and V = C \ {p}. We check each condition of lemma_54:

(a) U = C is a regular noetherian scheme. Since C is a smooth projective curve over the finite field k, it is in particular a regular (all local rings are regular local rings) and noetherian (finite type over a noetherian base) scheme.

(b) Z = {p} is a regular closed subscheme of U. The point p is a closed point of the smooth curve C. The local ring O_{C,p} is a discrete valuation ring (regular local ring of dimension 1), and the closed subscheme {p} is defined by the maximal ideal m_p of O_{C,p}. Since O_{C,p}/m_p = κ(p) is a field, the closed subscheme Spec(κ(p)) = {p} is regular (its only local ring is the field κ(p), which is regular of dimension 0).

(c) V = U \ Z = C \ {p} is the open complement.

(d) n > 1 by hypothesis.

All conditions of lemma_54 are satisfied.

Step 2: Identify the K-groups of Z.
The closed subscheme Z = {p} is Spec(κ(p)), where κ(p) is the residue field of p. Since C is a curve over the finite field k and p is a closed point, κ(p) is a finite extension of k, hence κ(p) is itself a finite field.

Step 3: Apply lemma_14 to κ(p).
By lemma_14 (with k replaced by the finite field κ(p)), for every integer m > 0 we have K_m(κ(p))⊗_Z Q = 0.
Since n > 1, we have n ≥ 2 > 0, so K_n(κ(p))⊗_Z Q = 0.
Since n > 1, we have n - 1 ≥ 1 > 0, so K_{n-1}(κ(p))⊗_Z Q = 0.

Step 4: Apply the exact sequence from lemma_54.
By lemma_54, the sequence
K_n(Z)⊗_Z Q → K_n(U)⊗_Z Q → K_n(V)⊗_Z Q → K_{n-1}(Z)⊗_Z Q
is exact, where the maps are induced by the inclusion Z ↪ U and the restriction U → V.
Substituting U = C, Z = Spec(κ(p)), V = C\{p}, and using Step 3, this becomes
0 → K_n(C)⊗_Z Q → K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q → 0.

Step 5: Conclude the isomorphism.
From the exactness of the sequence 0 → K_n(C)⊗_Z Q → K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q → 0, we deduce:
- The map K_n(C)⊗_Z Q → K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q is injective (its kernel is the image of the zero map 0 → K_n(C)⊗_Z Q, which is 0).
- The map K_n(C)⊗_Z Q → K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q is surjective (its image is the kernel of the zero map K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q → 0, which is all of K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q).

Therefore K_n(C)⊗_Z Q ≅ K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q as Q-vector spaces, via the restriction map induced by the open immersion C\{p} ↪ C. This completes the proof.

lemma_58.statement: Let f\colon X' \to X be a finite locally free morphism of rank r \ge 1 between regular noetherian schemes, and let n > 0. If the class of the vector bundle f_*\mathcal{O}_{X'} in K_0(X) equals r\cdot[\mathcal{O}_X], then the composite of f^{*}\colon K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(X')\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} with the transfer f_*\colon K_n(X')\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} is multiplication by r.
lemma_58.proof:
We prove the statement in the integral form (the composite is multiplication by $r$ already on $K_n(X)$), and then extend scalars to $\mathbf Q$. None of the previously proved lemmas is needed; the argument uses only the formalism of Quillen $K$-theory of exact categories together with the sheaf-theoretic projection formula, each step of which is justified below.

=== Notation and exact categories ===
Write $\mathrm{Vect}(X)$ for the exact category of algebraic vector bundles on $X$: short exact sequences are sequences $0\to E'\to E\to E''\to 0$ which are exact as sequences of $\mathcal O_X$-modules (equivalently, exact and with all terms locally free). We set $K_n(X):=K_n(\mathrm{Vect}\,X)$ in the sense of Quillen's $Q$-construction, $K_n(\mathcal C)=\pi_{n+1}(B Q\mathcal{\mathcal C})$ for $n\ge 0$; since $X$ and $X'$ are regular noetherian, the resolution theorem identifies this with the $K$-theory of coherent sheaves, so this is the usual $K$-theory of $X$. Analogously for $X'$.

=== Step 1: the transfer $f_*:K_n(X')\to K_n(X)$ is induced by an exact functor ===
A finite morphism is affine, so $f_*:\mathrm{QCoh}(X')\to\mathrm{QCoh}(X)$ is exact (affine-locally it is restriction of scalars along a ring map). We check it preserves vector bundles of finite rank. Let $\mathrm{Spec}\,A\subseteq X$ be affine; since $f$ is affine, $f^{-1}(\mathrm{Spec}\,A)=\mathrm{Spec}\,B$ with $B$ a finite locally free $A$-algebra of rank $r$. If $\mathcal F$ corresponds to a finite projective $B$-module $P$, then $P$ is a direct summand of $B^{m}$ as a $B$-module for some $m$, hence also as an $A$$-$module; since $B^{m}$ is finite free over $A$, $P$ is a finite projective $A$-module, i.e. $f_*\mathcal F$ is a vector bundle on $\mathrm{Spec}\,A$. Thus $f_*$ restricts to an exact functor
$$f_*^{\mathrm{VB}}:\mathrm{Vect}(X')\longrightarrow \mathrm{Vect}(X),\qquad \mathcal F\longmapsto f_*\mathcal F,$$
and the transfer in the statement is by definition the induced homomorphism of abelian groups $K_n(f_*^{\mathrm{VB}}):K_n(X')\to K_n(X)$ (which, under the resolution-theorem identifications, is the usual push-forward for the proper morphism $f$, because $f_*$ of a vector bundle is locally free and hence $K_n(\mathrm{Vect}\,X)\xrightarrow{\sim}K_n(\mathrm{Coh}\,X)$ intertwines the two constructions). Note also that $f_*^{\mathrm{VB}}(\mathcal O_{X'})=f_*\mathcal O_{X'}$, which is a vector bundle of rank $r$ by hypothesis.

=== Step 2: the pullback $f^*:K_n(X)\to K_n(X')$ ===
$f$ is finite locally free, hence flat, so $f^*$ is exact on $\mathcal O$-modules, and $f^*$ of a vector bundle is a vector bundle. Hence $f^{*,\mathrm{VB}}:\mathrm{Vect}(X)\to\mathrm{Vect}(X')$ is an exact functor and $f^*=K_n(f^{*,\mathrm{VB}})$.

=== Step 3 (structural fact: $K$-theory is invariant under natural isomorphism of exact functors) ===
Let $F,G:\mathcal C\rightleftarrows\mathcal D$ be exact functors of small exact categories and $\eta:F\Rightarrow G$ a natural isomorphism. Then $F$ and $G$ induce the same map $K_n(\mathcal C)\to K_n(\mathcal D)$ for every $n\ge0$. Proof: (a) For each $X\in\mathcal C$, $\eta_X:FX\to GX$ is a morphism of $Q\mathcal D$ (a roof $FX\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }FX\to GX$, or simply the image of a morphism of $\mathcal D$). The family $(\eta_X)$ is natural as a transformation $QF\Rightarrow QG$: for a morphism of $Q\mathcal C$ represented by a roof $X\xleftarrow{u}Y\xrightarrow{v}Z$ one must check $\eta_Z\circ QF(u,v)=QG(u,v)\circ\eta_X$ in $Q\mathcal D$. The left side is the roof $FX\leftarrow FY\to GZ$; the right side is the composite of $FX\to GX$ with $GX\leftarrow GY\to GZ$, i.e. $FX\leftarrow FX\times_{GX}GY\to GZ$. The canonical map $FY\to FX\times_{GX}GY$ induced by $F(u)$ and $\eta_Y$ is an isomorphism: indeed the square $FY\to GY$, $\downarrow\ \ \downarrow$, $FX\to GX$ commutes by naturality of $\eta$ and its two horizontal arrows are isomorphisms, whence for $x\in F(X),g\in G(Y)$ (in the concrete/elementwise notation, which is legitimate since the assertion is checked in any abelian envelope, e.g. by the Freyd embedding, or by a direct universal-property argument) the pair $(x,g)$ satisfies $\eta_X(x)=G(u)(g)$, so $g=\eta_Y(F(u)^{-1}x)$ uniquely. Thus the two roofs agree. (b) A natural transformation between functors gives a homotopy between the induced maps of nerves (it is a functor $\mathcal C\times[1]\to\mathcal D$ and $|N[1]|=\Delta^1$), so $BQF\simeq BQG$, and homotopic maps induce the same homomorphism on all homotopy groups. Hence $K_n(F)=K_n(G)$. $\triangleleft_{\!3}$

=== Step 4 (structural fact: the $K_0$-module structure on $K_n$) ===
We use the standard facts about the product in the Quillen $K$-theory of a scheme, which is induced by the bi-exact tensor-product functor $\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}:\mathrm{Vect}(X)\times\mathrm{Vect}(X)\to\mathrm{Vect}(X)$ (Quillen, "Higher algebraic $K$-theory I"; equivalently the symmetric-monoidal structure on exact categories and the lax-monoidal structure of the $K$-theory spectrum functor). For a scheme $Y$ these give:
(i) $K_*(Y)$ is a graded-commutative unital ring with unit $1=[\mathcal O_Y]\in K_0(Y)$;
(ii) for every vector bundle $E$ on $Y$ and every $\alpha\in K_n(Y)$ one has $[E]\cdot\alpha=(T_E)_*(\alpha)$, where $T_E:=E\otimes_{\mathcal O_Y}(-):\mathrm{Vect}(Y)\to\mathrm{Vect}(Y)$ (this is exactly how the pairing induced by a bi-exact functor behaves when the first variable is fixed at an object in degree $0$);
(iii) the product is $\mathbf Z$-bilinear.
For completeness we explain the two points on which (ii) rests, since they are the only non-elementary inputs. First, $E\mapsto (T_E)_*$ is additive for direct sums: $T_{E\oplus E'}\cong T_E\oplus T_{E'}$ naturally, and the map induced by the objectwise direct sum of two exact functors is the sum of the induced maps, because the addition on $K_n$ is induced by the biproduct functor $\oplus:\mathrm{Vect}\times\mathrm{Vect}\to\mathrm{Vect}$ (the $H$-space multiplication on $B Q\mathrm{Vect}$ coming from $\oplus$ agrees with the group law by the Eckmann–Hilton argument, so $m_*(a,b)=a+b$). Second, $E\mapsto (T_E)_*$ respects the conflation relations: given a short exact sequence $0\to E'\to E\to E''\to0$ in $\mathrm{Vect}(Y)$ and $\mathcal F\in\mathrm{Vect}(Y)$, the sequence $0\to E'\otimes\mathcal F\to E\otimes\mathcal F\to E''\otimes\mathcal F\to0$ is exact (the original sequence is locally split because $E''$ is locally free, and exactness may be checked locally), so $T_{E'}\to T_E\to T_{E''}$ is an objectwise short exact sequence of exact functors; Quillen's additivity theorem then gives $(T_E)_*=(T_{E'})_*+(T_{E''})_*$. Hence $E\mapsto (T_E)_*$ factors through $K_0(Y)$, which is the content of (ii) together with the identification of the resulting action with the product from (i). We also record that there is no left/right ambiguity: $T_E\cong T'_E$ with $T'_E(\mathcal F)=\mathcal F\otimes E$ by the natural isomorphism $E\otimes\mathcal F\cong\mathcal F\otimes E$, so by Step 3 left and right multiplication by $[E]$ coincide.
Consequences we shall use: $[\mathcal O_Y]\cdot\alpha=\alpha$ for all $\alpha$, and by $\mathbf Z$-bilinearity $(m[\mathcal O_Y])\cdot\alpha=m\,\alpha$ for all $m\in\mathbf Z$.

=== Step 5: the projection formula as a natural isomorphism of exact endofunctors of $\mathrm{Vect}(X)$ ===
Consider the two exact endofunctors of $\mathrm{Vect}(X)$
$$\Phi:=f^{\mathrm{VB}}_*\circ f^{*,\mathrm{VB}},\qquad \Psi:=T_{f_*\mathcal O_{X'}}=f_*\mathcal O_{X'}\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}(-).$$
(Both are exact: $f^*$ is exact because $f$ is flat, $f_*$ is exact because $f$ is affine, and tensoring with a locally free sheaf is exact.) We construct a natural isomorphism $\theta:\Psi\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\Phi$. Let $\varepsilon:f^*f_*\mathcal O_{X'}\to\mathcal O_{X'}$ be the counit of the adjunction $(f^*,f_*)$. For $\mathcal F\in\mathrm{Vect}(X)$ define
$$\psi_{\mathcal F}:f^*\big(f_*\mathcal O_{X'}\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}\mathcal F\big)\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;f^*f_*\mathcal O_{X'}\otimes_{\mathcal O_{X'}}f^*\mathcal F\;\xrightarrow{\;\varepsilon\otimes\mathrm{id}\;}\;\mathcal O_{X'}\otimes_{\mathcal O_{X'}}f^*\mathcal F\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;f^*\mathcal F,$$
using that $f^*$ commutes with tensor products, and let $\theta_{\mathcal F}$ be the adjoint morphism $f_*\mathcal O_{X'}\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}\mathcal F\to f_*f^*\mathcal F$. Every ingredient is functorial in $\mathcal F$, so $\theta$ is a natural transformation of functors $\mathrm{Vect}(X)\to\mathrm{Vect}(X)$.
We check $\theta_{\mathcal F}$ is an isomorphism on an affine open cover. Take $\mathrm{Spec}\,A\subseteq X$ with $f^{-1}(\mathrm{Spec}\,A)=\mathrm{Spec}\,B$; then $B$ is finite locally free of rank $r$ over $A$, and $\mathcal F|_{\mathrm{Spec}\,A}=\widetilde M$ with $M$ a finite projective $A$-module. We have $f_*\mathcal O_{X'}|_{\mathrm{Spec}\,A}=\widetilde B$, $f^*\mathcal F|_{\mathrm{Spec}\,B}=\widetilde{B\otimes_A M}$ (a $B$-module), hence $\Psi(\mathcal F)|_{\mathrm{Spec}\,A}=\widetilde{B\otimes_A M}$ and $\Phi(\mathcal F)|_{\mathrm{Spec}\,A}=\widetilde{B\otimes_A M}$ (as $A$-modules). Under these identifications $\varepsilon$ is the multiplication map $B\otimes_A B\to B$, $b_1\otimes b_2\mapsto b_1b_2$, so $\psi_{\mathcal F}$ is $b_1\otimes(b_2\otimes m)\mapsto b_1b_2\otimes m$. The adjoint $\theta_{\mathcal F}$ is the $A$-linear endomorphism of $B\otimes_A M$ given by $x\mapsto\psi_{\mathcal F}(1\otimes x)$, i.e. $b\otimes m\mapsto 1\cdot b\otimes m=b\otimes m$: the identity. Hence $\theta_{\mathcal F}$ is an isomorphism, and $\theta:\Psi\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\Phi$ is a natural isomorphism of exact functors.
By Step 3, $\Psi$ and $\Phi$ induce the same homomorphism on $K_n(X)$:
$$f_*\circ f^*\;=\;K_n(\Phi)\;=\;K_n(\Psi)\;=\;(T_{f_*\mathcal O_{X'}})_*\qquad\text{as endomaps of }K_n(X). \tag{$\ast$}$$

=== Step 6: conclusion over $\mathbf Z$ ===
Let $\alpha\in K_n(X)$. Using ($\ast$) and then Step 4(ii) with $E=f_*\mathcal O_{X'}$, then the hypothesis $[f_*\mathcal O_{X'}]=r\cdot[\mathcal O_X]$ in $K_0(X)$, then Step 4(iii) and the unit property:
$$f_*\big(f^*(\alpha)\big)=(T_{f_*\mathcal O_{X'}})_*(\alpha)=[f_*\mathcal O_{X'}]\cdot\alpha=(r[\mathcal O_X])\cdot\alpha=r\,\big([\mathcal O_X]\cdot\alpha\big)=r\,\alpha.$$
Thus the composite $K_n(X)\xrightarrow{f^*}K_n(X')\xrightarrow{f_*}K_n(X)$ is multiplication by $r$, as endomorphisms of the abelian group $K_n(X)$ (valid for every $n\ge0$, in particular for $n>0$).

=== Step 7: extension of scalars to $\mathbf Q$ ===
The two maps in the statement are the $\mathbf Q$-linear extensions $f^*\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf Q}$ and $f_*\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf Q}$ of the integral maps, since $-\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ is a functor on abelian groups. Every element of $K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ is a finite sum $\sum_i\alpha_i\otimes q_i$, and
$$\big(f_*\otimes\mathrm{id}\big)\big(f^*\otimes\mathrm{id}\big)\Big(\textstyle\sum_i\alpha_i\otimes q_i\Big)=\sum_i f_*f^*(\alpha_i)\otimes q_i=\sum_i r\alpha_i\otimes q_i=r\sum_i\alpha_i\otimes q_i,$$
using Step 6 in the middle equality. Hence the composite on $K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ is multiplication by $r$. Since $r\ge1$, $r$ is invertible in $\mathbf Q$, so (although not required by the statement) $f^*$ is injective and $f_*$ is surjective on rational $K$-theory in every degree $n>0$.

=== Remark (equivalent formulation) ===
The same conclusion is the $\beta=1$ instance of the general projection formula $f_*(f^*x\cdot y)=x\cdot f_*y$ for $x\in K_m(X)$, $y\in K_n(X')$: with $y=[\mathcal O_{X'}]\in K_0(X')$ one gets $f_*f^*x=x\cdot f_*[\mathcal O_{X'}]=x\cdot[f_*\mathcal O_{X'}]=r\,x$. We gave the argument above in the form $f_*f^*=T_{f_*\mathcal O_{X'}}$ because it reduces the projection formula to the elementary sheaf-level computation of Step 5 plus the functoriality of Step 3.

This completes the proof. (Regularity/noetherianity of $X,X'$ is used only to work in the standard framework where $K$-theory of vector bundles agrees with $K$-theory of coherent sheaves, so that "the transfer" is the usual one; the computation itself takes place entirely in the exact categories of vector bundles.)

lemma_62.statement: Let F \subset F' be a field extension of finite degree d > 0, and let n > 0. If K_n(F')\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0, then K_n(F)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0.
lemma_62.proof:
We prove the statement by identifying the two fields with the spectra of rings and applying the projection-formula-type statement of lemma_58 (eoinm/lemma_58), which gives that pullback followed by transfer is multiplication by the rank.

Step 1: Reformulation as a statement about schemes.
Put X = Spec F and X' = Spec F'. For a field k, every vector bundle on Spec k is a finite free k-module, and the exact category of vector bundles on Spec k is exactly the exact category of finite-dimensional k-vector spaces; hence by definition K_n(Spec k) = K_n(k) for all n >= 0. Thus the desired conclusion is K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0, and the hypothesis is K_n(X') \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0.

The inclusion F \subset F' is a homomorphism of rings, hence gives a morphism f: X' = Spec F' \to X = Spec F.

Step 2: Verification that f is finite locally free of rank d.
Since F' is a field extension of F of finite degree d, F' is a d-dimensional vector space over F; choosing an F-basis of F' gives an isomorphism of F-modules F' \cong F^{\oplus d}. In particular F' is a finitely generated (indeed free) F-module, so f is finite; and f_*\mathcal O_{X'} is the \mathcal O_X-module associated to F' viewed as an F-vector space, which is free of rank d. Since X = Spec F consists of a single point, "free" and "locally free" agree, so f is finite locally free of constant rank r = d. Note that no separability hypothesis is used: only that F' is free of rank d over F.

Step 3: Verification that X and X' are regular noetherian.
A field is noetherian (its only ideals are 0 and itself). The scheme Spec F has a single point, whose local ring is F itself, a regular local ring of dimension 0 (global dimension 0 = Krull dimension 0). Hence X is regular and noetherian; the same argument applies to X'. Also r = d \ge 1 by hypothesis (d > 0), and n > 0 by hypothesis.

Step 4: Verification of the K_0 hypothesis of lemma_58.
For a field F, K_0(Spec F) is the Grothendieck group of the monoid of isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional F-vector spaces under direct sum; the rank (dimension) map identifies this monoid with (\mathbf N, +) and hence K_0(Spec F) with \mathbf Z, in such a way that [\mathcal O_X] = [F] maps to 1. The class [f_*\mathcal O_{X'}] maps to dim_F F' = d. Therefore [f_*\mathcal O_{X'}] = d \cdot [\mathcal O_X] in K_0(X) = K_0(Spec F), as required.

Step 5: Application of lemma_58.
All hypotheses of lemma_58 (eoinm/lemma_58) are now satisfied with X = Spec F, X' = Spec F', and r = d. It yields that the composite
\[ K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{\;f^*\;} K_n(X')\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{\;f_*\;} K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \]
is multiplication by d. Written in terms of fields, the composite
\[ K_n(F)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{\;f^*\;} K_n(F')\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{\;f_*\;} K_n(F)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \]
satisfies f_*(f^*(x)) = d\,x for every x \in K_n(F)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q.

(Concretely: f^* is induced by the exact extension-of-scalars functor F' \otimes_F -, and f_* by the exact restriction-of-scalars functor; their composite is the exact functor P \mapsto (F'\otimes_F P) viewed as an F-vector space, which is naturally isomorphic to P^{\oplus d}, and by Quillen's additivity this induces multiplication by d — this is exactly the content of lemma_58 that we invoke.)

Step 6: Conclusion.
By hypothesis K_n(F')\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q = 0, i.e. it is the zero \mathbf Q-vector space. Hence for every x \in K_n(F)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q we have f^*(x) = 0, and since f_* is a homomorphism of \mathbf Q-vector spaces it sends 0 to 0. Thus
\[ d\,x \;=\; f_*(f^*(x)) \;=\; f_*(0) \;=\; 0 \qquad \text{for all } x. \]
Now K_n(F)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q is a \mathbf Q-vector space and d is a positive integer, so d \neq 0 in \mathbf Q and multiplication by d is an automorphism, with inverse multiplication by 1/d \in \mathbf Q. Given x, we obtain
\[ x = 1 \cdot x = \tfrac{1}{d}\,(d x) = \tfrac{1}{d}\cdot 0 = 0. \]
Hence every element of K_n(F)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q is zero, i.e. K_n(F)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q = 0.

This proves the lemma for every field extension F \subset F' of finite degree d > 0 and every n > 0, with no separability assumption required.

lemma_63.statement: Let k be a finite field, let f\colon X' \to X be a finite locally free morphism of degree d > 0 between smooth projective varieties over k, and suppose the class of f_*\mathcal{O}_{X'} in K_0(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} equals d\cdot[\mathcal{O}_X]. If K_n(X')\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0 for some n > 0, then K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0.
lemma_63.proof:
Write $A := K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ and $A' := K_n(X')\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$; by hypothesis $A'=0$. We must show $A=0$. The only formal input is lemma_58, which asserts that for a finite locally free morphism $h\colon W\to V$ of rank $r\ge 1$ between regular noetherian schemes with $[h_*\mathcal O_W]=r\cdot[\mathcal O_V]$ **in** $K_0(V)$, the composite $h_*\circ h^*$ on $K_n(V)\otimes\mathbf Q$ is multiplication by $r$. Our hypothesis gives the equality only after tensoring with $\mathbf Q$, so we first replace $f$ by a morphism for which the equality holds integrally.

Step 1: Clearing the denominators. Let $\gamma := [f_*\mathcal O_{X'}]-d\cdot[\mathcal O_X]\in K_0(X)$. The assumption is that $\gamma$ maps to $0$ in $K_0(X)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q = S^{-1}K_0(X)$ with $S=\mathbf Z\setminus\{0\}$. Since a fraction $\gamma/1$ vanishes in a localization iff $s\gamma=0$ for some $s\in S$, there is an integer $m\ge 1$ with $m\gamma=0$ in $K_0(X)$, i.e.
$$m\,[f_*\mathcal O_{X'}] \;=\; md\,[\mathcal O_X]\qquad\text{in } K_0(X).\tag{1}$$
(If the original equality already holds integrally one may take $m=1$; nothing below changes.)

Step 2: The $m$-fold copy of $f$. Let $Y:=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{m} X'_i$ be the disjoint union of $m$ copies $X'_i\simeq X'$ of $X'$, and let $g\colon Y\to X$ be the morphism whose restriction to $X'_i$ is $f$ for every $i$. We check the properties of $g$.

(2a) $g$ is finite locally free of rank $md$. Finiteness and local freeness can be checked on affine opens of $X$: let $V=\operatorname{Spec}R\subset X$ be affine. Since $f$ is finite locally free of degree $d$, $f^{-1}V=\operatorname{Spec}S$ with $S$ an $R$-algebra that is a locally free $R$-module of rank $d$. Then $g^{-1}V=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^m\operatorname{Spec}S=\operatorname{Spec}(S\times\cdots\times S)$, and the product ring $S^m:=S\times\cdots\times S$ ($m$ factors) is, as an $R$-module, the direct sum $S^{\oplus m}$, hence locally free of rank $md$. Thus $g$ is finite locally free of rank $md$, and $g_*\mathcal O_Y\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m} f_*\mathcal O_{X'}$ as $\mathcal O_X$-modules (indeed $g_*\mathcal O_Y(U)=\mathcal O_Y(g^{-1}U)=\prod_i\mathcal O_{X'}(f^{-1}U)=\bigoplus_i f_*\mathcal O_{X'}(U)$, the product being finite).

(2b) $X$ and $Y$ are regular noetherian schemes. $X$ and $X'$ are smooth of finite type over the field $k$, hence noetherian and regular (a smooth algebra over a field is regular). A finite disjoint union of regular noetherian schemes is regular noetherian, so $Y$ is regular noetherian.

(2c) The integral class condition. In $K_0(X)$, addition is induced by direct sum of vector bundles, so $[g_*\mathcal O_Y]=\big[\bigoplus_{i=1}^m f_*\mathcal O_{X'}\big]=\sum_{i=1}^m [f_*\mathcal O_{X'}]=m[f_*\mathcal O_{X'}]$, which by (1) equals $md\,[\mathcal O_X]$. Thus the class of $g_*\mathcal O_Y$ in $K_0(X)$ is exactly $r\cdot[\mathcal O_X]$ with $r:=md\ge 1$.

Step 3: The $K$-theory of $Y$ vanishes rationally in degree $n$. Each $X'_i$ is open and closed in $Y$, so restriction to the components gives an equivalence of exact categories $\mathrm{Vect}(Y)\xrightarrow\sim\prod_{i=1}^m \mathrm{Vect}(X'_i)$ (quasi-inverse: extend a bundle on $X'_i$ by $0$ along the open-and-closed immersion $X'_i\hookrightarrow Y$, which is exact and preserves vector bundles). By the product theorem for Quillen $K$-theory, $K_n(Y)\cong\prod_{i=1}^m K_n(X'_i)=\bigoplus_{i=1}^m K_n(X'_i)$ (finite product $=$ finite direct sum). Tensoring with $\mathbf Q$, which is additive and commutes with finite direct sums, gives
$$K_n(Y)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{i=1}^m\big(K_n(X'_i)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q\big)=\bigoplus_{i=1}^m A'=0,$$
the last equality since each $X'_i\simeq X'$ and $A'=0$ by hypothesis.

Step 4: Apply lemma_58 to $g$. Since $g\colon Y\to X$ is finite locally free of rank $r=md\ge 1$ between regular noetherian schemes, $[g_*\mathcal O_Y]=md\,[\mathcal O_X]$ in $K_0(X)$, and $n>0$, lemma_58 applies and says that the composite
$$K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{\;g^*\;} K_n(Y)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{\;g_*\;} K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$$
is multiplication by $md$.

Step 5: Conclude. By Step 3 the middle term is $0$, so $g^*\colon A\to 0$ is the zero map, hence the composite $g_*\circ g^*\colon A\to A$ is the zero endomorphism. By Step 4 this endomorphism is also $a\mapsto md\cdot a$. Thus $md\cdot a=0$ for every $a\in A$. But $A$ is a $\mathbf Q$-vector space and $md$ is a nonzero integer, so $md$ acts invertibly, with inverse the action of $1/(md)\in\mathbf Q$. Hence for every $a\in A$,
$$a=\tfrac{1}{md}\,(md\cdot a)=\tfrac{1}{md}\cdot 0=0.$$
Therefore $A=K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0$, which is the claim.

Remark on the role of the hypotheses: smoothness of $X,X'$ is used only to make them regular noetherian (the standing hypothesis of lemma_58); the degree condition $d>0$ is used to ensure $r=md\ge 1$ and that $md$ acts invertibly on $A$; and $n>0$ is the range of lemma_58.

lemma_64.statement: Let k be a finite field and X a smooth quasi-projective scheme over k. Suppose X admits a finite decreasing filtration by closed subschemes X = Z_0 \supseteq Z_1 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq Z_m = \emptyset such that each Z_i is smooth over k and each locally closed subscheme Z_i \setminus Z_{i+1} is isomorphic to a finite disjoint union of affine spaces over k. Then K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0 for every n > 1.
lemma_64.proof:
We work with Quillen K-theory of vector bundles: for a scheme Y of finite type over k we write K_q(Y) := π_q of the K-theory space of the exact category Vect(Y) of algebraic vector bundles on Y. Fix once and for all an integer q > 1; at the end q is arbitrary, which will give the statement for every n > 1.

STEP 0 (Preliminaries: empty scheme, additivity, extension of scalars).

(F1) K_q(∅) = 0. Indeed, Vect(∅) is the zero exact category (there is exactly one object, the empty bundle, and it is zero), so its K-theory space is contractible and all its homotopy groups vanish.

(F2) Additivity for finite disjoint unions. If Y = \coprod_{j=1}^{s} Y_j is a finite disjoint union of schemes, the restriction maps along the open-and-closed inclusions ι_j : Y_j → Y induce an isomorphism K_q(Y) →≅ ⊕_{j=1}^{s} K_q(Y_j).
Proof. Since each ι_j is simultaneously open and closed, restriction gives an equivalence of exact categories Vect(Y) →≅ ∏_{j=1}^{s} Vect(Y_j): the inverse sends (E_j)_j to the sheaf ⊕_j (ι_j)_*E_j, which is a vector bundle because (ι_j)_* = extension by zero is exact for an open-and-closed immersion, and the two constructions are visibly mutually inverse (a sheaf on a disjoint union is a tuple of sheaves on the pieces). Quillen's construction Q/S_• of the K-theory space commutes with finite products of exact categories (products are computed degreewise, and group completion of a finite product of simplicial abelian groups/Γ-spaces is the product), and π_q of a product of spaces is the product of the π_q. Hence K_q(Y) ≅ ∏_j K_q(Y_j), and a finite product of abelian groups is their direct sum. ∎

(F3) The ring Q is a flat Z-algebra, and −⊗_Z Q commutes with finite direct sums: (⊕_j A_j)⊗_Z Q ≅ ⊕_j (A_j⊗_Z Q) for abelian groups A_j.

STEP 1 (Affine spaces).
We claim K_q(A^r_k)⊗_Z Q = 0 for every r ≥ 0.
• If r ≥ 1, then A^r_k = Spec k[t_1,…,t_r], and lemma_38 of eoinm ("k finite field, r a positive integer, n > 1 ⇒ K_n(k[t_1,…,t_r])⊗Q = 0") applied with n = q > 1 gives K_q(k[t_1,…,t_r])⊗_Z Q = 0.
• If r = 0, then A^0_k = Spec k, and lemma_14 of eoinm ("k finite field, n > 0 ⇒ K_n(k)⊗Q = 0") applied with n = q gives K_q(k)⊗_Z Q = 0.

STEP 2 (The strata have rationally trivial K_q).
For each i ∈ {0,…,m−1} set W_i := Z_i \ Z_{i+1}, viewed as the open subscheme of Z_i (equivalently the given locally closed subscheme of X). By hypothesis W_i ≅ \coprod_{j=1}^{s_i} A^{r_{ij}}_k for some s_i ≥ 0 and r_{ij} ≥ 0. If s_i ≥ 1, then by (F2), (F3) and Step 1,
K_q(W_i)⊗_Z Q ≅ ( ⊕_{j=1}^{s_i} K_q(A^{r_{ij}}_k) ) ⊗_Z Q ≅ ⊕_{j=1}^{s_i} ( K_q(A^{r_{ij}}_k)⊗_Z Q ) = 0.
If s_i = 0 then W_i = ∅ and (F1) gives K_q(W_i) = 0. Thus for all i:
  (∗)   K_q(W_i)⊗_Z Q = 0.

STEP 3 (Regularity and noetherianity of the pieces).
Each Z_i is smooth over k, hence of finite type over the field k, hence noetherian. Moreover each Z_i is regular: for a point z ∈ Z_i, the local ring O_{Z_i,z} is smooth over k, so by the standard structure of smooth morphisms there is an étale local k-algebra map k[t_1,…,t_d] → O_{Z_i,z} at a point of A^d_k (d = dim_z Z_i); the ring k[t_1,…,t_d] is regular (its local rings at maximal ideals are regular local rings, of dimension equal to the minimal number of generators of the maximal ideal, by Noether normalisation together with the fact that a monic extension of a regular ring is regular in the unramified-in-codimension-1 sense; equivalently, the local ring at a closed point is a localisation of a finite monic extension of a polynomial ring, hence regular), and regularity is preserved under étale localisation (an étale local ring of a regular local ring is regular, since it is a filtered colimit of smooth — in particular regular — algebras, and regularity is stable under such filtered colimits). Hence O_{Z_i,z} is regular, so Z_i is regular.

STEP 4 (Closed immersions inside the filtration).
For each i, Z_{i+1} is a closed subscheme of Z_i. Indeed, closed subschemes of X correspond to quasi-coherent ideal sheaves; writing I_j ⊂ O_X for the ideal of Z_j, the inclusions Z_0 ⊇ Z_1 ⊇ … of closed subschemes mean I_0 ⊆ I_1 ⊆ … ⊆ I_m = O_X. Then Z_{i+1} is the closed subscheme of Z_i = Spec_{O_X}(O_X/I_i) defined by the quasi-coherent ideal I_{i+1}/I_i ⊂ O_X/I_i, and the complement of this closed subscheme in Z_i is exactly W_i = Z_i \ Z_{i+1}. By Step 3, Z_{i+1} is regular.

STEP 5 (Downward induction on the filtration).
For i ∈ {0,…,m} let P(i) be the statement "K_q(Z_i)⊗_Z Q = 0".
• Base case i = m: Z_m = ∅, so K_q(Z_m) = 0 by (F1) and P(m) holds.
• Inductive step: assume P(i+1). We apply lemma_51 of eoinm ("U noetherian, Z a regular closed subscheme, V = U \ Z, n > 0: K_n(Z)⊗Q = 0 and K_n(V)⊗Q = 0 ⇒ K_n(U)⊗Q = 0") with U := Z_i, Z := Z_{i+1}, V := W_i and n := q. Its hypotheses are verified:
   – U = Z_i is noetherian (Step 3);
   – Z = Z_{i+1} is a regular closed subscheme of U (Steps 3 and 4);
   – V = U \ Z = W_i (Step 4);
   – n = q > 1 > 0;
   – K_q(Z)⊗Q = K_q(Z_{i+1})⊗Q = 0 by the induction hypothesis P(i+1);
   – K_q(V)⊗Q = K_q(W_i)⊗Q = 0 by (∗).
  Lemma_51 then yields K_q(Z_i)⊗_Z Q = 0, i.e. P(i). (Concretely, this is the exactness of the localisation sequence K_q(Z_{i+1}) → K_q(Z_i) → K_q(W_i) → K_{q-1}(Z_{i+1}) after tensoring with Q: the outer terms vanish rationally, so the middle one does too.)
By descending induction, P(i) holds for every i = 0,1,…,m.

STEP 6 (Conclusion).
P(0) says K_q(Z_0)⊗_Z Q = 0, and Z_0 = X by hypothesis. Thus K_q(X)⊗_Z Q = 0. Since q > 1 was arbitrary, K_n(X)⊗_Z Q = 0 for every n > 1, which is the claim.

(Remark on the hypotheses: smoothness of X and quasi-projectivity are used only to guarantee that the pieces Z_i are noetherian and that the Z_{i+1} ⊂ Z_i are regular closed subschemes, so that lemma_51 applies at each step; the rational vanishing of K_q on the cells comes from lemma_38 / lemma_14, i.e. from Quillen's computation of the K-theory of a finite field together with homotopy invariance for polynomial rings over finite fields.)

lemma_67.statement: Let $k$ be a finite field, let $d$ be a positive integer and let $n>0$. Then $K_n(\mathbf{P}^d_k)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0$.
lemma_67.proof:
Let $k$ be a finite field and let $n>0$ be an integer. We prove, by induction on $d\ge 0$, that $K_n(\mathbf P^d_k)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0$; the required statement (where $d$ is a positive integer) is then the case $d\ge 1$. We treat $n=1$ and $n>1$ separately, since the input lemmas have different ranges.

**Case $n=1$.** For every $d\ge 0$ the scheme $\mathbf P^d_k$ is smooth and projective over the finite field $k$. Lemma 32 of eoinm ("$k$ finite field, $X$ smooth projective over $k$ $\Rightarrow$ $K_1(X)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0$") applies with $X=\mathbf P^d_k$ and gives $K_1(\mathbf P^d_k)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0$. This settles $n=1$ for all $d$, with no induction needed.

**Case $n>1$.** Fix such an $n$; we induct on $d$.

*Base step $d=0$.* $\mathbf P^0_k=\operatorname{Spec} k$, so $K_n(\mathbf P^0_k)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=K_n(k)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$, which is $0$ by lemma 14 of eoinm (finite field $k$, $n>0$). \checkmark

*Inductive step.* Let $d\ge 1$ and assume $K_n(\mathbf P^{d-1}_k)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0$. We verify the hypotheses of lemma 51 of eoinm (localisation: $U$ noetherian, $Z\subset U$ a regular closed subscheme, $V=U\setminus Z$, $m>0$; if $K_m(Z)\otimes\mathbf Q=0$ and $K_m(V)\otimes\mathbf Q=0$ then $K_m(U)\otimes\mathbf Q=0$) with
$$U=\mathbf P^d_k,\qquad Z=\mathbf P^{d-1}_k\ (\text{the standard linear hyperplane}),\qquad V=U\setminus Z,\qquad m=n.$$

(1) *$Z$ is a closed subscheme of $U$ with complement $\mathbf A^d_k$.* Write $\mathbf P^d_k=\operatorname{Proj} k[x_0,\dots,x_d]$. The homogeneous ideal $\mathfrak a=(x_d)$ defines the closed subscheme $V_+(x_d)=\operatorname{Proj} k[x_0,\dots,x_d]/(x_d)=\operatorname{Proj} k[x_0,\dots,x_{d-1}]=\mathbf P^{d-1}_k$, and the induced immersion $i:\mathbf P^{d-1}_k\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^d_k$, $[x_0:\dots:x_{d-1}]\mapsto[x_0:\dots:x_{d-1}:0]$, is a closed immersion. Its complement is the basic open $D_+(x_d)=(\operatorname{Proj} k[x_0,\dots,x_d])_{x_d}=\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(k[x_0,\dots,x_d,x_d^{-1}]_0\bigr)$. The degree-zero part of the localisation is the polynomial ring $k[x_0/x_d,\dots,x_{d-1}/x_d]$ in the $d$ variables $y_j:=x_j/x_d$ ($j=0,\dots,d-1$): every element of the localisation is a fraction $f/x_d^{\deg f}$ with $f$ homogeneous of degree $\deg f$, which is a polynomial in the $y_j$, and these $y_j$ are algebraically independent over $k$ because the $x_j$ are. Hence $V\cong\operatorname{Spec} k[y_0,\dots,y_{d-1}]=\mathbf A^d_k$.

(2) *$i$ is a regular closed immersion.* Cover $U$ by the standard affines $U_j=D_+(x_j)$, $j=0,\dots,d$. On $U_j$ with $j\neq d$, the ideal sheaf of $Z$ is generated by the image of $x_d$, i.e. by $y_d:=x_d/x_j$, which is one of the polynomial coordinates of $\mathcal O_U(U_j)\cong k[x_0/x_j,\dots,x_d/x_j]$, a polynomial ring over a field and hence a domain; a nonzero element of a domain is a non-zero-divisor, so $y_d$ is a non-zero-divisor. On $U_d$ the ideal restricts to the unit ideal (indeed $Z\cap U_d=\varnothing$), generated by $1$, again a non-zero-divisor. Thus $\mathcal I_Z$ is locally generated by a single non-zero-divisor, i.e. $Z$ is an effective Cartier divisor, so $i$ is a regular closed immersion and $Z$ is a regular closed subscheme of $U$. (In particular $Z$ is regular, agreeing with the fact that $\mathbf P^{d-1}_k$ is smooth over $k$.)

(3) *$U$ is noetherian.* $\mathbf P^d_k$ is of finite type over the field $k$, hence a noetherian scheme.

(4) *Vanishing on $Z$.* $K_n(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=K_n(\mathbf P^{d-1}_k)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0$ by the induction hypothesis.

(5) *Vanishing on $V$.* By (1), $V=\operatorname{Spec} k[t_1,\dots,t_d]$ with $d\ge 1$ a positive integer, and $n>1$; lemma 38 of eoinm (finite field $k$, $r\ge 1$, $n>1$: $K_n(k[t_1,\dots,t_r])\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0$) applied with $r=d$ gives $K_n(V)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0$.

Applying lemma 51 with $m=n>0$ to the triple $Z\subset U$, $V=U\setminus Z$, and using (2), (3), (4), (5), we conclude $K_n(\mathbf P^d_k)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0$. This completes the inductive step.

By induction, $K_n(\mathbf P^d_k)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0$ for all $d\ge 0$ and all $n>1$; together with the case $n=1$ handled by lemma 32, the same holds for all $n>0$. In particular, for every positive integer $d$ and every $n>0$,
$$K_n(\mathbf P^d_k)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0,$$
which is the claim.

(Remark on the logic: the argument is the usual cellular-filtration/localisation induction — $\mathbf P^d_k$ is obtained from $\mathbf P^{d-1}_k$ by gluing the affine cell $\mathbf A^d_k$, whose rational $K$-theory vanishes by homotopy invariance together with the Quillen–Suslin vanishing for $k$; lemma 51 packages the relevant piece of the localisation long exact sequence rationally, and only the same-degree terms $K_n(Z)\to K_n(U)\to K_n(V)$ are needed, so no induction on $n$ is required.)

lemma_66.statement: Let $R$ be a discrete valuation ring essentially of finite type over a finite field $k$, with fraction field $F$ and finite residue field $\kappa$. Then for every integer $n\ge 2$ the homomorphism $K_n(R)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q\to K_n(F)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ induced by the inclusion $R\subset F$ is an isomorphism of $\mathbf Q$-vector spaces.
lemma_66.proof:
We prove the statement in five steps. Throughout, write $M_{\mathbf Q}:=M\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ for an abelian group $M$, and $K_m(Y):=K_m(\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y))$ for an affine scheme $Y$.

**Step 1. $R$ is noetherian, and its prime spectrum has exactly two points.**
By hypothesis $R$ is essentially of finite type over $k$: there are a finitely generated $k$-algebra $A$ and a multiplicative set $S\subset A$ with $R\simeq S^{-1}A$. By the Hilbert basis theorem $A$ is noetherian, and localisations of noetherian rings are noetherian, so $R$ is noetherian.

$R$ is a discrete valuation ring: a local domain with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m=(\pi)$ generated by a single non-zero element $\pi$ which is not a unit, and such that every non-zero $x\in R$ has the form $x=u\pi^{v(x)}$ with $u\in R^{*}$ and $v(x)\ge 0$. Let $\mathfrak p\ne(0)$ be a prime ideal of $R$, and choose $0\ne x=u\pi^{m}\in\mathfrak p$ with $m=v(x)\ge 0$. Since $u$ is a unit and $\mathfrak p$ is prime, $\pi^{m}\in\mathfrak p$ forces $\pi\in\mathfrak p$ (and $m\ge 1$ because $x\ne 0$ in a domain and $u$ is a unit). Hence $\mathfrak m=(\pi)\subseteq\mathfrak p$, so $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak m$. Thus $\operatorname{Spec}R=\{(0),\mathfrak m\}$ and $\kappa=R/\mathfrak m=R/(\pi)$ is the residue field at $\mathfrak m$, finite by hypothesis.

**Step 2. $U:=\operatorname{Spec}R$ is a regular noetherian scheme.**
Noetherianity is Step 1. For regularity we check each local ring: $R_{(0)}$ is the fraction field $F$, a field, hence regular; and $R_{\mathfrak m}=R$ is a local noetherian ring whose maximal ideal is generated by one element $\pi$ while $\dim R=1$ (the only chains of primes are $(0)\subsetneq\mathfrak m$), so the minimal number of generators of $\mathfrak mR_{\mathfrak m}$ equals $\dim R_{\mathfrak m}$, i.e. $R_{\mathfrak m}$ is regular local. Hence $U$ is regular noetherian.

**Step 3. $Z:=V(\pi)$ is a regular closed subscheme of $U$, and $U\setminus Z\simeq\operatorname{Spec}F$ with the open immersion given by $R\subset F$.**
$Z=V(\pi)$ is the closed subscheme defined by the ideal sheaf $\widetilde{(\pi)}$; since $\mathfrak m=(\pi)$, the underlying set is $\{\mathfrak m\}$ and $Z=\operatorname{Spec}(R/(\pi))=\operatorname{Spec}\kappa$. The single point of $Z$ is $\mathfrak m$, and in $R_{\mathfrak m}=R$ the element $\pi$ is a non-zero-divisor because $R$ is a domain and $\pi\ne0$; so the ideal $(\pi)$ is generated by a regular sequence of length one at every point of $Z$, i.e. the closed immersion $i\colon Z\hookrightarrow U$ is a regular immersion. Moreover $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\kappa$ is the spectrum of a field, hence regular. Thus $Z$ is a regular closed subscheme of $U$ in the sense required by eoinm:lemma_54.

For the complement: as a set, $U\setminus Z=D(\pi)=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R:\pi\notin\mathfrak p\}=\{(0)\}$, and scheme-theoretically $D(\pi)=\operatorname{Spec}R_{\pi}$. The canonical map $R_{\pi}\to F$ is an isomorphism: it is injective because $x/1=0$ in $R_\pi$ means $\pi^{j}x=0$ for some $j\ge0$, and $R$ is a domain with $\pi\neq0$, so $x=0$; it is surjective because a general element $a/b\in F$ with $b\ne0$ has $b=u\pi^{m}$, so $a/b=(a\,u^{-1}\pi^{-m})/1\in R_{\pi}$. Under this identification $U\setminus Z\simeq\operatorname{Spec}F$, the open immersion $j\colon U\setminus Z\hookrightarrow U$ corresponds contravariantly to the localisation homomorphism $R\to R_{\pi}$, $x\mapsto x/1$, which under $R_{\pi}\simeq F$ is exactly the given inclusion $R\subset F$. Consequently the "restriction" map $K_n(U)_{\mathbf Q}\to K_n(U\setminus Z)_{\mathbf Q}$ of the localisation sequence is precisely the map $K_n(R)_{\mathbf Q}\to K_n(F)_{\mathbf Q}$ induced by $R\subset F$ that the lemma is about.

**Step 4. Rational vanishing of the $K$-groups of $Z$.**
The residue field $\kappa$ is finite by hypothesis, so eoinm:lemma_14 applies to the finite field $\kappa$: $K_m(\kappa)_{\mathbf Q}=0$ for every integer $m>0$. Since $n\ge2$, both $n>0$ and $n-1>0$; therefore
$$K_n(Z)_{\mathbf Q}=K_n(\kappa)_{\mathbf Q}=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad K_{n-1}(Z)_{\mathbf Q}=K_{n-1}(\kappa)_{\mathbf Q}=0.$$

**Step 5. Apply the rational localisation sequence and conclude.**
We may apply eoinm:lemma_54 to the regular noetherian scheme $U=\operatorname{Spec}R$, its regular closed subscheme $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\kappa$, the open complement $V=U\setminus Z=\operatorname{Spec}F$ (Step 3), and the integer $n$, which satisfies $n>1$ because $n\ge2$. It yields an exact sequence of $\mathbf Q$-vector spaces
$$K_n(Z)_{\mathbf Q}\longrightarrow K_n(U)_{\mathbf Q}\longrightarrow K_n(V)_{\mathbf Q}\longrightarrow K_{n-1}(Z)_{\mathbf Q},$$
that is, by Steps 3--4,
$$0\longrightarrow K_n(R)_{\mathbf Q}\xrightarrow{\ \varphi\ }K_n(F)_{\mathbf Q}\longrightarrow 0,$$
where $\varphi$ is the map induced by the inclusion $R\subset F$. Exactness at $K_n(R)_{\mathbf Q}$ says $\ker\varphi=\operatorname{im}(0\to K_n(R)_{\mathbf Q})=0$, so $\varphi$ is injective; exactness at $K_n(F)_{\mathbf Q}$ says $\operatorname{im}\varphi=\ker(K_n(F)_{\mathbf Q}\to 0)=K_n(F)_{\mathbf Q}$, so $\varphi$ is surjective. The map $\varphi$ is $\mathbf Q$-linear because it is obtained by extending scalars to $\mathbf Q$ from the group homomorphism $K_n(R)\to K_n(F)$. Hence $\varphi\colon K_n(R)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }K_n(F)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ is an isomorphism of $\mathbf Q$-vector spaces, for every $n\ge2$. $\blacksquare$

**Remarks on the hypotheses and edge cases (not part of the proof).**
(a) The assumption that $\kappa$ is finite is exactly what Step 4 consumes, via eoinm:lemma_14; it is *not* a consequence of "essentially of finite type over $k$". Indeed $R=k[x,y]_{(x)}$ is a DVR essentially of finite type over $k$ with fraction field $k(x,y)$ and residue field $k(y)$, which is infinite, and the conclusion fails there: the boundary map $\partial\colon K_2(k(x,y))\to k(y)^{*}$ of the localisation sequence is the tame symbol, it is surjective since $\partial\{x,\tilde u\}=u$ for any unit $u\in k(y)^{*}$ lifted to a unit $\tilde u\in R^{*}$, while $k(y)^{*}\to R^{*}$ is zero because $R^{*}\to F^{*}$ is injective; thus $\operatorname{coker}(K_2(R)_{\mathbf Q}\to K_2(F)_{\mathbf Q})$ contains the nonzero group $k(y)^{*}\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ (e.g. the class of $y$ has infinite order).
(b) The restriction $n\ge2$ is sharp for this argument: eoinm:lemma_54 requires $n>1$, and for $n=1$ the sequence $K_1(R)_{\mathbf Q}\to K_1(F)_{\mathbf Q}\to K_0(\kappa)_{\mathbf Q}$ has cokernel $\kappa^{*}\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$, which need not vanish even for finite $\kappa$ replaced by an infinite residue field, so no isomorphism is claimed at $n=1$.
(c) The proof actually shows the slightly more general fact that the conclusion holds for any DVR with finite residue field; the "essentially of finite type over $k$" hypothesis is used only to guarantee noetherianity of $R$ (Step 1), which is part of the standing hypotheses of the lemma.

lemma_73.statement: Let k be a finite field, let t be an indeterminate, and let n > 1. Then K_n(k(t)) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.
lemma_73.proof: Proof. For each nonzero f in k[t] set R_f = k[t, 1/f]. If f divides g, there is a natural inclusion R_f -> R_g; for any f, g the polynomial fg is an upper bound, so (R_f)_{f != 0} is a filtered direct system. Its colimit in rings is k(t). Indeed, each R_f is a subring of k(t), and every element x of k(t) can be written as p/q with p, q in k[t] and q != 0, hence x lies in R_q. We use the standard filtered-colimit theorem for Quillen K-theory: if A = colim_i A_i is a filtered colimit of rings, then for every n >= 1 the natural map colim_i K_n(A_i) -> K_n(A) is an isomorphism. Applying it to A_i = R_f gives K_n(k(t)) ≅ colim_{f != 0} K_n(R_f). The field Q is flat over Z (it is a localization of Z), so tensoring with Q commutes with filtered colimits. Therefore K_n(k(t)) ⊗_Z Q ≅ colim_{f != 0} (K_n(R_f) ⊗_Z Q). (1) Now fix f != 0. Factor f as c ∏_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i} with c ∈ k^× and p_1, ..., p_r distinct monic irreducible polynomials in k[t]. Let B_f be the finite set of closed points V(p_1), ..., V(p_r) of A^1_k. The prime ideals of R_f = k[t, 1/f] are exactly the prime ideals of k[t] that do not contain f; these are the zero ideal and the maximal ideals (q) with q a monic irreducible not among the p_i. Hence Spec R_f is the open subscheme A^1_k minus B_f. By lemma_47 (eoinm, lemma_47), since k is a finite field and n > 1, K_n(A^1_k minus B_f) ⊗_Z Q = 0. Thus K_n(R_f) ⊗_Z Q = 0 for this f. Since f was arbitrary, every term in the filtered colimit in (1) is zero. A filtered colimit of zero abelian groups is zero. Hence the right-hand side of (1) is zero, and by (1) K_n(k(t)) ⊗_Z Q = 0. This proves the lemma.

lemma_78.statement: Let k be a field, let X be a closed subscheme of \mathbf{P}^N_k, and let H be a hyperplane in \mathbf{P}^N_k. Then the open subscheme X \setminus (X \cap H) is an affine scheme.
lemma_78.proof:
Let S = k[x_0, ..., x_N] and write P^N_k = Proj S. A hyperplane H in P^N_k is the zero scheme of a nonzero linear form. Since k is a field, any nonzero linear form can be completed to a basis of the dual vector space, so after a linear change of homogeneous coordinates we may assume that H = V_+(x_0). Affineness is invariant under isomorphism, so it is enough to treat this coordinate case.

Let I ⊂ S be a homogeneous ideal such that X = Proj(S/I), and put R = S/I. The scheme-theoretic intersection X ∩ H is V_+((x_0)) inside X, equivalently Proj(R/(x_0)). Therefore the open complement of X ∩ H in X is the open subscheme
D_+(x_0) ∩ Proj R.

The standard affine chart D_+(x_0) of P^N_k is isomorphic to A^N_k. Explicitly, the degree-zero part of S_{x_0} is
S_{(x_0)} = k[x_1/x_0, ..., x_N/x_0],
and the usual construction of Proj identifies D_+(x_0) with Spec S_{(x_0)}. For completeness, the point correspondence is Q ↦ {s homogeneous in S : s/x_0^{deg s} ∈ Q}, with inverse P ↦ P_{x_0} ∩ S_{(x_0)}; closed sets correspond by V_+(J) ∩ D_+(x_0) ↔ V(J_{x_0} ∩ S_{(x_0)}), and on stalks the local ring of D_+(x_0) at P is (S_P)_0, which is isomorphic to (S_{(x_0)})_{P_{x_0} ∩ S_{(x_0)}} via y_i ↦ x_i/x_0.

Under this chart isomorphism, the closed subscheme D_+(x_0) ∩ Proj R is the closed subscheme of Spec S_{(x_0)} defined by the image of I. Its coordinate ring is
R_{(x_0)} = (R_{x_0})_0.
Because R is generated in degree 1 by the images of x_0, ..., x_N, the map
k[y_1, ..., y_N] → R_{(x_0)}, y_i ↦ x_i/x_0,
is surjective. Hence R_{(x_0)} ≅ k[y_1, ..., y_N]/J for some ideal J (possibly the unit ideal, in which case the scheme is empty). Thus
D_+(x_0) ∩ Proj R ≅ Spec(k[y_1, ..., y_N]/J),
which is affine.

Therefore the open complement of X ∩ H in X is affine. If the original hyperplane is not the coordinate hyperplane, we have applied an automorphism of P^N_k, so the conclusion holds in general.

lemma_73_primitive_11_anti_self_dual.statement: Let M be a Kähler surface, let Ω be its Kähler form, and let α be a real (1,1)-form on M such that Ω∧α = 0. Then *α = -α.
lemma_73_primitive_11_anti_self_dual.proof:
We prove the pointwise statement. Both the hypothesis Ω∧α = 0 and the conclusion *α = -α are fiberwise (pointwise) conditions: Ω∧α = 0 means the 4-form vanishes at every point, and *α = -α means the two 2-forms agree at every point. Hence it suffices to fix p ∈ M and work entirely in the cotangent space T_p^*M.

Step 1 (unitary coframe). Since (M,Ω) is Kähler, the metric g = g_Ω is Hermitian and compatible with the complex structure J. Choose a g-orthonormal unitary basis e_1, e_2 of T_p^{1,0}M and let θ_1, θ_2 be the dual (1,0)-coframe, written θ_j = dx_j + i dy_j with dx_j, dy_j real 1-forms. In this coframe the Kähler form is Ω_p = (i/2)(θ_1∧θ̄_1 + θ_2∧θ̄_2). Because θ_1∧θ̄_1 = (dx_1+i dy_1)∧(dx_1-i dy_1) = -2i dx_1∧dy_1 (and likewise for index 2), we obtain Ω_p = dx_1∧dy_1 + dx_2∧dy_2. The Riemannian volume form, with the orientation induced by the complex structure (so (e_1, Je_1, e_2, Je_2) is positive), is vol_p = dx_1∧dy_1∧dx_2∧dy_2.

Step 2 (basis of real (1,1)-forms). Set ω_1 = dx_1∧dy_1, ω_2 = dx_2∧dy_2, σ = dx_1∧dx_2 + dy_1∧dy_2, τ = dx_1∧dy_2 - dy_1∧dx_2. The complex (1,1)-forms are spanned by θ_1∧θ̄_1 = -2iω_1, θ_2∧θ̄_2 = -2iω_2, θ_1∧θ̄_2 = σ - iτ, θ_2∧θ̄_1 = σ + iτ; therefore the real (1,1)-forms are exactly the real span of {ω_1, ω_2, σ, τ}. (The two remaining real 2-forms, dx_1∧dx_2 - dy_1∧dy_2 and dx_1∧dy_2 + dy_1∧dx_2, equal Re(θ_1∧θ_2) and Im(θ_1∧θ_2), which are of type (2,0)+(0,2), not (1,1).) Consequently α_p = aω_1 + bω_2 + cσ + dτ for unique a,b,c,d ∈ ℝ.

Step 3 (primitivity). Compute Ω_p∧α_p. Since 2-forms commute under the wedge product, ω_1∧ω_1 = ω_2∧ω_2 = 0 and ω_1∧ω_2 = ω_2∧ω_1 = vol_p. Also (ω_1+ω_2)∧σ = ω_1∧σ + ω_2∧σ = 0 and (ω_1+ω_2)∧τ = 0, because every summand repeats a 1-form factor (e.g. ω_1∧σ = dx_1∧dy_1∧dx_1∧dx_2 + dx_1∧dy_1∧dy_1∧dy_2 = 0, and ω_2∧τ = dx_2∧dy_2∧dx_1∧dy_2 - dx_2∧dy_2∧dy_1∧dx_2 = 0). Hence Ω_p∧α_p = (ω_1+ω_2)∧(aω_1+bω_2+cσ+dτ) = (a+b)vol_p. Evaluating the hypothesis Ω∧α = 0 at p gives (a+b)vol_p = 0, so a + b = 0, i.e. α_p = a(ω_1 - ω_2) + cσ + dτ.

Step 4 (Hodge star). Let {ω_1, e_1, e_2, e_3, e_4, ω_2} be the orthonormal basis of Λ²T_p^*M with e_1 = dx_1∧dx_2, e_2 = dx_1∧dy_2, e_3 = dy_1∧dx_2, e_4 = dy_1∧dy_2. The Hodge star on 2-forms is the unique linear map satisfying β∧(*γ) = ⟨β,γ⟩vol_p for all 2-forms β,γ; uniqueness holds because if β∧η = 0 for every β, then testing β against the orthonormal basis forces η = 0. We claim *ω_1 = ω_2, *ω_2 = ω_1, *σ = -σ, *τ = -τ. We verify the defining relation for each basis β (the orthonormality gives ⟨β,γ⟩ = δ_{βγ}):
• γ = ω_1, *γ = ω_2: for β = ω_1, ω_1∧ω_2 = vol_p = ⟨ω_1,ω_1⟩vol_p; for β = ω_2, e_1, e_2, e_3, e_4 the form β∧ω_2 has a repeated 1-factor (ω_2∧ω_2 = 0, e_1∧ω_2 = dx_1∧dx_2∧dx_2∧dy_2 = 0, e_4∧ω_2 = dy_1∧dy_2∧dx_2∧dy_2 = 0, e_2∧ω_2 = dx_1∧dy_2∧dx_2∧dy_2 = 0, e_3∧ω_2 = dy_1∧dx_2∧dx_2∧dy_2 = 0), matching ⟨β,ω_1⟩ = 0.
• γ = ω_2, *γ = ω_1: for β = ω_2, ω_2∧ω_1 = vol_p; for the other five β, β∧ω_1 = 0 by the same repeated-factor argument.
• γ = σ = e_1+e_4, *γ = -σ: for β = σ, σ∧(-σ) = -σ∧σ, and σ∧σ = (e_1+e_4)∧(e_1+e_4) = e_1∧e_4 + e_4∧e_1 = -vol_p - vol_p = -2vol_p (since e_1∧e_4 = dx_1∧dx_2∧dy_1∧dy_2 = -vol_p), so σ∧(-σ) = 2vol_p = ⟨σ,σ⟩vol_p. For β = e_1, e_1∧(-σ) = -(e_1∧e_4) = vol_p = ⟨e_1,σ⟩vol_p; for β = e_4, e_4∧(-σ) = -(e_4∧e_1) = vol_p = ⟨e_4,σ⟩vol_p; for β ∈ {ω_1,ω_2,e_2,e_3}, β∧σ = 0 = ⟨β,σ⟩vol_p.
• γ = τ = e_2 - e_3, *γ = -τ: for β = τ, τ∧(-τ) = -τ∧τ, and τ∧τ = (e_2-e_3)∧(e_2-e_3) = -e_2∧e_3 - e_3∧e_2 = -vol_p - vol_p = -2vol_p (since e_2∧e_3 = dx_1∧dy_2∧dy_1∧dx_2 = vol_p and e_3∧e_2 = dy_1∧dx_2∧dx_1∧dy_2 = vol_p), so τ∧(-τ) = 2vol_p = ⟨τ,τ⟩vol_p. For β = e_2, e_2∧(-τ) = -(e_2∧e_2 - e_2∧e_3) = vol_p = ⟨e_2,τ⟩vol_p; for β = e_3, e_3∧(-τ) = -(e_3∧e_2 - e_3∧e_3) = -vol_p = ⟨e_3,τ⟩vol_p; for β ∈ {ω_1,ω_2,e_1,e_4}, β∧τ = 0 = ⟨β,τ⟩vol_p.
Thus the claimed star values hold.

Step 5 (conclusion). By linearity and Step 4, *α_p = a(*ω_1 - *ω_2) + c*σ + d*τ = a(ω_2 - ω_1) - cσ - dτ = -[a(ω_1 - ω_2) + cσ + dτ] = -α_p. As p ∈ M was arbitrary, *α = -α on M. ∎

lemma_79.statement: Let k be a field, let X be a smooth projective variety over k, and let D \subset X be an effective Cartier divisor such that the invertible sheaf \mathcal{O}_X(D) is very ample. Then the open complement of the support of D in X is an affine scheme.
lemma_79.proof: Proof. If X is empty, then U is empty and affine. Assume X is nonempty. Set L = O_X(D) and V = H^0(X,L). Then V is finite dimensional. Since L is very ample, the evaluation map ev: V tensor O_X -> L is surjective; in particular V is nonzero, because at any point x of X the fiber map V tensor k(x) -> L tensor k(x) is surjective onto a one-dimensional nonzero space. Let N = dim V - 1 and identify P(V^vee) with P^N_k. The surjection ev defines a morphism phi: X -> P^N_k; because L is very ample, phi is a closed immersion, phi^*O(1) is canonically isomorphic to L, and the induced map H^0(P^N_k,O(1)) = V -> H^0(X,L) = V is the identity. Let s_D be the canonical section of L whose zero scheme is D. It is nonzero: if s_D were zero, its zero scheme would be X, so D = X, but the ideal sheaf of X in X is 0, which is not an invertible sheaf on the nonempty scheme X. Let ell in V be the unique element whose pullback is s_D; ell is nonzero. If N = 0, then P^0_k = Spec k and phi is a closed immersion X -> Spec k. Since X is nonempty, X is isomorphic to Spec k. The ideal sheaf of a closed subscheme of Spec k is either 0 or O; for an effective Cartier divisor it must be invertible, and 0 is not invertible, so the divisor is empty. Hence U = X is affine. Now assume N >= 1. Let H = V_+(ell) in P^N_k, the hyperplane defined by the linear form ell. The scheme-theoretic preimage under phi of H is the zero scheme of the pulled-back section phi^*ell = s_D, hence is D. Let Y = phi(X) be the closed subscheme of P^N_k isomorphic to X. Then Y cap H corresponds to D, and the open complement of Supp(D) in X is isomorphic to the open subscheme Y minus (Y cap H). By lemma_78, Y minus (Y cap H) is affine. Affineness is invariant under isomorphism, so U is affine.

lemma_82_laurent_n_ge_3.statement: Let k be a finite field, let d be a positive integer, let t_1,...,t_d be indeterminates, and let n ≥ 3. Then K_n(k[t_1,...,t_d,t_d^{-1}]) ⊗_Z Q = 0.
lemma_82_laurent_n_ge_3.proof:
Let k be a finite field, let d be a positive integer, let t_1,...,t_d be indeterminates, and let n >= 3. We prove that K_n(k[t_1,...,t_d,t_d^{-1}]) tensor_Z Q = 0.

Step 1: Define the geometric objects. Let U = A^d_k = Spec k[t_1,...,t_d]. This is a smooth affine variety over k of dimension d >= 1. Let Z = V(t_d) be the closed subscheme of U cut out by the single equation t_d = 0. Since t_d is a non-zero-divisor in the polynomial ring k[t_1,...,t_d], the ideal (t_d) is a regular ideal of height 1, so Z is a smooth hypersurface in U. Concretely, Z = Spec k[t_1,...,t_d]/(t_d) = Spec k[t_1,...,t_{d-1}], which is smooth over k (it is affine space of dimension d-1 if d >= 2, or a single point Spec k if d = 1). Let V = U \setminus Z = D(t_d) = Spec k[t_1,...,t_d,t_d^{-1}]. This is exactly the scheme whose K-theory group we want to show vanishes after tensoring with Q.

Step 2: Apply lemma_52. We have: k is a finite field; U is a smooth affine variety over k of dimension d >= 1; Z is a smooth hypersurface in U; and n >= 3 > 1. The only remaining hypotheses of lemma_52 are that K_n(Z) tensor_Z Q = 0 and K_{n-1}(Z) tensor_Z Q = 0. We verify these in the next step.

Step 3: Verify the vanishing of K_n(Z) tensor Q and K_{n-1}(Z) tensor Q. We split into two cases.

Case d = 1: Then Z = Spec k[t_1]/(t_1) = Spec k, a single point. So K_n(Z) = K_n(k) and K_{n-1}(Z) = K_{n-1}(k). By lemma_14, for any m > 0 we have K_m(k) tensor_Z Q = 0. Since n >= 3 > 0, K_n(Z) tensor_Z Q = K_n(k) tensor_Z Q = 0. Since n >= 3, we have n-1 >= 2 > 0, so K_{n-1}(Z) tensor_Z Q = K_{n-1}(k) tensor_Z Q = 0 by lemma_14.

Case d >= 2: Then Z = Spec k[t_1,...,t_{d-1}], where d-1 >= 1 is a positive integer. By lemma_38, for any positive integer r and any m > 1, we have K_m(k[t_1,...,t_r]) tensor_Z Q = 0. Since n >= 3 > 1, K_n(Z) tensor_Z Q = K_n(k[t_1,...,t_{d-1}]) tensor_Z Q = 0 by lemma_38 with r = d-1 and m = n. Since n >= 3, we have n-1 >= 2 > 1, so K_{n-1}(Z) tensor_Z Q = K_{n-1}(k[t_1,...,t_{d-1}]) tensor_Z Q = 0 by lemma_38 with r = d-1 and m = n-1.

In both cases, the hypotheses of lemma_52 are satisfied.

Step 4: Conclude from lemma_52. By lemma_52, K_n(U) tensor_Z Q is isomorphic to K_n(U \setminus Z) tensor_Z Q = K_n(V) tensor_Z Q as Q-vector spaces.

Step 5: Show K_n(U) tensor_Z Q = 0. We have U = Spec k[t_1,...,t_d] with d >= 1 a positive integer and n >= 3 > 1. By lemma_38 with r = d and m = n, K_n(k[t_1,...,t_d]) tensor_Z Q = 0, i.e., K_n(U) tensor_Z Q = 0.

Step 6: Final conclusion. From Step 4, K_n(V) tensor_Z Q is isomorphic to K_n(U) tensor_Z Q. From Step 5, K_n(U) tensor_Z Q = 0. Therefore K_n(V) tensor_Z Q = 0. Since V = Spec k[t_1,...,t_d,t_d^{-1}], we have K_n(k[t_1,...,t_d,t_d^{-1}]) tensor_Z Q = 0, as required.

lemma_83.statement: Let k be a finite field, let C be a smooth projective geometrically integral curve over k, let F be its function field, and let n > 1. Then K_n(C)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q is isomorphic to K_n(F)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q as \mathbf Q-vector spaces.
lemma_83.proof:
Let n>1. Since C is a projective curve over a finite field, it has infinitely many closed points; choose two distinct closed points p and q. Let U be the open complement of q in C. The divisor q has positive degree, so for some m≥1 the line bundle O_C(mq) is very ample. By lemma_79, U is affine. Let A=Γ(U). Then A is a regular noetherian domain of dimension 1, essentially of finite type over k, and its fraction field is F. The closed point p corresponds to a maximal ideal m_p of A.

By lemma_55 applied to C and q, the restriction map gives an isomorphism K_n(C)⊗_Z Q ≅ K_n(U)⊗_Z Q = K_n(A)⊗_Z Q. (1)

We next prove K_n(A)⊗_Z Q ≅ K_n(A_{m_p})⊗_Z Q. Let S be the complement of m_p in A. The local ring A_{m_p} is the filtered colimit of the rings A_f for f∈S: for f,g∈S, h=fg∈S gives maps A_f→A_h and A_g→A_h, and every element a/s with s∈S lies in A_s. We use the standard fact that Quillen K-theory commutes with filtered colimits of rings. For completeness, if R=colim R_i is a filtered colimit, then GL(R)=colim GL(R_i) as groups, hence BGL(R)=colim BGL(R_i) as simplicial sets; homotopy groups commute with filtered colimits of simplicial sets, and the plus construction is compatible with filtered colimits, so K_n(R)≅colim K_n(R_i). Tensoring with Q also commutes with filtered colimits. Therefore K_n(A_{m_p})⊗_Z Q ≅ colim_{f∈S} K_n(A_f)⊗_Z Q.

For any f∈S, the map A→A_f corresponds to the open immersion Spec A_f=D(f)→Spec A. The complement is the reduced closed subscheme Z_f=V(f)_{red}, a finite set of closed points of the regular curve Spec A, hence a regular closed subscheme. Applying lemma_54 to U=Spec A, Z=Z_f, V=Spec A_f gives an exact sequence K_n(Z_f)⊗_Z Q → K_n(A)⊗_Z Q → K_n(A_f)⊗_Z Q → K_{n-1}(Z_f)⊗_Z Q. The scheme Z_f is a finite disjoint union of spectra of finite fields, so by additivity of K-theory and lemma_14 both K_n(Z_f)⊗_Z Q and K_{n-1}(Z_f)⊗_Z Q are zero (here n>1, so n-1>0). Thus K_n(A)⊗_Z Q → K_n(A_f)⊗_Z Q is an isomorphism for every f∈S.

Consequently the canonical map K_n(A)⊗_Z Q → colim_{f∈S} K_n(A_f)⊗_Z Q is an isomorphism. Surjectivity follows because every element of the colimit comes from some K_n(A_f) and K_n(A)→K_n(A_f) is surjective after tensoring with Q. For injectivity, if an element of K_n(A) maps to zero in the colimit, then by the standard description of filtered colimits of abelian groups it maps to zero in some K_n(A_f); since K_n(A)→K_n(A_f) is injective after tensoring with Q, the element was zero. Hence K_n(A)⊗_Z Q ≅ K_n(A_{m_p})⊗_Z Q. (2)

The ring A_{m_p} is the local ring O_{C,p}. It is a DVR, essentially of finite type over k, with fraction field F and finite residue field κ(p). By lemma_66, K_n(A_{m_p})⊗_Z Q ≅ K_n(F)⊗_Z Q. (3)

Combining (1), (2), and (3) gives an isomorphism of Q-vector spaces K_n(C)⊗_Z Q ≅ K_n(F)⊗_Z Q, as required.

lemma_83_simplicial_colimit_homotopy.statement: Let I be a filtered category, let (X_i)_{i∈I} be a diagram of simplicial sets, let X = colim_{i∈I} X_i, let x_i be compatible vertices of X_i whose image in X is a vertex x, and let |−| denote geometric realization. Then for every integer n ≥ 1, the natural map colim_{i∈I} π_n(|X_i|, x_i) → π_n(|X|, x) induced by the canonical maps X_i → X is an isomorphism.
lemma_83_simplicial_colimit_homotopy.proof:
Proof.
Notation. For a morphism i -> j in I write p_{ij}:X_i -> X_j, and for the canonical map write p_i:X_i -> X. Composition is p_{jk} p_{ij}=p_{ik}. The colimit X is computed degreewise. Hence a simplex of X_m is represented by a simplex in (X_i)_m for some i, and if two simplices from the same stage (X_i)_m have the same image in X_m, then for some morphism i -> j their images in (X_j)_m are equal. This is the standard filtered-colimit property for sets. The transition maps are based because p_{ij}(x_i)=x_j, so they induce homomorphisms pi_n(|X_i|,x_i) -> pi_n(|X_j|,x_j), and the maps to |X| induce the natural homomorphism from the colimit.
Step 1. Realization commutes with the filtered colimit. Geometric realization is left adjoint to the singular complex functor, so it preserves colimits. Therefore |X| is homeomorphic to the topological colimit colim_i |X_i|. Under this homeomorphism the map |p_i|:|X_i| -> |X| is the canonical map to the colimit. In particular the underlying set of |X| is the filtered colimit of the underlying sets of |X_i|.
Step 2. Compact subsets of realizations. For any simplicial set Y, |Y| is a CW complex. Its closed cells are the realizations of the nondegenerate simplices, and the closure of each closed cell is a finite union of closed cells (the faces). We prove that every compact subset K of |Y| is contained in a finite subcomplex.
Let E be the set of nondegenerate simplices sigma of Y such that K meets int |sigma|. We show E is finite. Suppose E is infinite. For each sigma in E choose a point a_sigma in K cap int |sigma|, and let A be the set of all a_sigma. For any closed cell bar tau, bar tau is a finite union of closed cells, so it contains the interiors of only finitely many cells. Hence A cap bar tau is finite. By the weak topology of a CW complex, a subset is closed if and only if its intersection with every closed cell is closed. Finite subsets of the Hausdorff spaces bar tau are closed, so A is closed in |Y|. Similarly, for each sigma in E, A minus {a_sigma} has finite intersection with every closed cell, so it is closed; hence {a_sigma} is open in A. Thus A is an infinite discrete space. Since A is closed in the compact space K, A is compact. This is impossible, because the cover of A by its singletons has no finite subcover. Therefore E is finite.
Every point of |Y| lies in the interior of a unique nondegenerate simplex. Consequently K is contained in the union of the finitely many closed cells bar sigma for sigma in E, which is a finite subcomplex.
We also record that if C is a simplicial subset of Y, then |C| is the subcomplex of |Y| spanned by the nondegenerate simplices of C, and the inclusion |C| -> |Y| is injective. Indeed, if a point y lies in |C|, then y is represented by some simplex c of C, and the unique nondegenerate simplex tau representing y is a face of c; since C is closed under faces, tau belongs to C.
Step 3. Finite embedding lemma. First we prove that every finite simplicial set is finitely presentable in sSet. Here finite means having finitely many nondegenerate simplices.
(a) Delta^m is finitely presentable. A map Delta^m -> colim_i X_i is determined by an m-simplex of colim_i X_i, and such a simplex is represented in some X_i.
(b) Let G be a pushout G = A union_D B, where A, B, and D are finite simplicial sets and A and B are finitely presentable. Then G is finitely presentable. Given g:G -> colim_i X_i, factor g|_A through some X_{i_A} and g|_B through some X_{i_B}. Choose i0 above i_A and i_B. We obtain maps u:A -> X_{i0} and v:B -> X_{i0} whose images in the colimit are g|_A and g|_B. The two composites D -> X_{i0} obtained from u and v have equal images in the colimit. Since D is finite, for each nondegenerate simplex d of D the corresponding simplices in X_{i0} have the same image in X, so by the filtered-colimit property there is a stage k_d above i0 where they agree. Taking a common stage i1 above all k_d, the maps p_{i0,i1}u and p_{i0,i1}v agree on the nondegenerate simplices of D, hence on all simplices. By the universal property of the pushout they define a map w:G -> X_{i1}, and p_{i1}w = g.
(c) Every finite simplicial set is finitely presentable. Induct on the number N of nondegenerate simplices. The empty case is trivial. For N>0 choose a nondegenerate simplex sigma of maximal degree m. Let F' be the simplicial subset spanned by all nondegenerate simplices except sigma. Let L be the subcomplex of Delta^m spanned by the proper faces of sigma. Both F' and L have fewer than N nondegenerate simplices (F contains sigma and all of its proper faces), so by induction they are finitely presentable. The map L -> F' is induced by the simplicial map Delta^m -> F that sends the canonical m-simplex to sigma; its image lies in F'. Then F is the pushout F' union_L Delta^m. By (b), F is finitely presentable.
Now let F be a finite simplicial subset of X and let i0 be any object of I. The inclusion u:F -> X is a map from a finitely presentable object to the filtered colimit, so by (c) there is i and a simplicial map e:F -> X_i with p_i e = u. If i is not above i0, replace i by an object i1 above i and i0 and replace e by p_{i,i1}e. The map e is a monomorphism: if e(a)=e(b), then a=u(a)=p_i e(a)=p_i e(b)=u(b). If F contains the basepoint vertex x, then e(x) and x_i are vertices of X_i with the same image x in X. By the filtered-colimit property for sets, choose j above i with p_{ij}(e(x))=p_{ij}(x_i)=x_j. Then e_j=p_{ij}e satisfies p_j e_j=u and e_j(x)=x_j, and it is a monomorphism. This proves the finite embedding lemma.
Step 4. Finite-image factorization lemma. Let C be a finite simplicial subset of X_j, let K be any topological space, and let a,b:K -> |C| be maps such that |p_j|a = |p_j|b. We prove that for some k above j, |p_{jk}|a = |p_{jk}|b.
Let W = p_j(C), the simplicial subset of X spanned by the images of the nondegenerate simplices of C. Since C is finite, W is finite. By the finite embedding lemma, choose l above j and a monomorphism e:W -> X_l such that p_l e is the inclusion W -> X. Let f:C -> W be the simplicial map f(rho)=p_j(rho).
For each nondegenerate simplex rho of C, the two simplices p_{jl}(rho) and e(f(rho)) of X_l have the same image in X. By the filtered-colimit property, choose k_rho above l such that p_{l,k_rho}(p_{jl}(rho)) = p_{l,k_rho}(e(f(rho))). Since C has finitely many nondegenerate simplices, choose k above l and all k_rho. Then the simplicial maps p_{jk}|_C and p_{lk} e f from C to X_k agree on all nondegenerate simplices, hence agree on all simplices, because every simplex is a degeneracy of a unique nondegenerate simplex. Therefore, as maps |C| -> |X_k|,
|p_{jk}| = |p_{lk}| |e| |f|.
On the other hand, p_j|_C is the composite C -> W -> X, so
|p_j| = |incl_W| |f|,
where incl_W:W -> X is the inclusion. The inclusion |W| -> |X| is injective by Step 2. Hence |p_j|a = |p_j|b implies |f|a = |f|b, and then
|p_{jk}|a = |p_{lk}| |e| |f|a = |p_{lk}| |e| |f|b = |p_{jk}|b.
This proves the finite-image factorization lemma.
Step 5. Surjectivity. Let [f] be an element of pi_n(|X|,x), n>=1. The map f:S^n -> |X| has compact image. By Step 2, there is a finite simplicial subset C of X containing f(S^n). Since f is based, x belongs to C. By the finite embedding lemma, choose i and a monomorphism e:C -> X_i with p_i e = inclusion and e(x)=x_i. Let f':S^n -> |C| be the corestriction of f. Then f = |p_i| |e| f', and f' is based at x_i. Thus [f] is the image in the colimit of the class of |e|f' in pi_n(|X_i|,x_i). This proves surjectivity.
Step 6. Injectivity. Let alpha be an element of colim_i pi_n(|X_i|,x_i) whose image in pi_n(|X|,x) is 0. Choose i and a based map f_i:S^n -> |X_i| representing alpha. Then |p_i|f_i is based null-homotopic in |X|. Choose a based homotopy H:S^n x I -> |X| with H(s,0)=|p_i|f_i(s), H(s,1)=x, and H(*,t)=x. The image of H is compact, so by Step 2 there is a finite simplicial subset C of X containing H(S^n x I); it contains x. By the finite embedding lemma with lower bound i, choose j above i and a monomorphism e:C -> X_j with p_j e = inclusion and e(x)=x_j. Let H':S^n x I -> |C| be the corestriction of H.
Define A:S^n -> |X_j| by A(s)=|e|H'(s,0), and define B:S^n -> |X_j| by B(s)=|p_{ij}|f_i(s). Then |p_j|A = |p_i|f_i = |p_j|B.
The images of A and B are compact in |X_j|. By Step 2 applied to X_j, choose finite simplicial subsets C_A and C_B of X_j containing A(S^n) and B(S^n), respectively. Let C' be the finite simplicial subset spanned by C_A, C_B, and x_j. Then A and B factor uniquely through |C'|: there are a',b':S^n -> |C'| such that A is the inclusion composed with a' and B is the inclusion composed with b'. The equality |p_j|A=|p_j|B gives |p_j|a' = |p_j|b' as maps into |X|. By Step 4, choose k above j such that |p_{jk}|a' = |p_{jk}|b'. Hence |p_{jk}|A = |p_{jk}|B.
Now define H_k:S^n x I -> |X_k| by H_k = |p_{jk}| |e| H'. This is a based homotopy, because H'(*,t)=x, e(x)=x_j, and p_{jk}(x_j)=x_k. At time 0,
H_k(s,0) = |p_{jk}|A(s) = |p_{jk}|B(s) = |p_{ik}|f_i(s).
At time 1, H_k(s,1)=x_k. Therefore |p_{ik}|f_i is based null-homotopic in |X_k|. Thus the class of f_i maps to 0 in pi_n(|X_k|,x_k), and consequently alpha is 0 in the colimit. This proves injectivity.
Combining Steps 5 and 6, the natural map colim_i pi_n(|X_i|,x_i) -> pi_n(|X|,x) is an isomorphism for every n>=1. QED.

lemma_85.statement: Let k be a finite field, let C be a smooth projective curve over k, let S be a finite set of closed points of C, and let n > 1. Then K_n(C) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} is isomorphic to K_n(C \setminus S) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} as \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces.
lemma_85.proof:
Proof. Let k be a finite field, let C be a smooth projective curve over k, let S be a finite set of closed points of C, and let n>1. We show that the restriction map j^* induced by the open immersion j: C\setminus S \hookrightarrow C is an isomorphism of Q-vector spaces K_n(C)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{\sim} K_n(C\setminus S)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q.

Step 1 (empty S). If S=\emptyset then C\setminus S = C and j^* is the identity map, so the assertion holds trivially.

Step 2 (removing the points one at a time). Assume S\neq\emptyset and write S={p_1,\dots,p_m} with m=|S|\ge 1. For 0\le i\le m set W_i = C\setminus\{p_1,\dots,p_i\} (with the empty set removed when i=0). Then W_0=C, W_m=C\setminus S, and W_{i+1}=W_i\setminus\{p_{i+1}\}.

Claim. For every i=0,\dots,m-1 the restriction map g_i: K_n(W_i)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to K_n(W_{i+1})\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q is an isomorphism of Q-vector spaces.

Proof of the claim. Fix i\in\{0,\dots,m-1\} and put Z_i=\{p_{i+1}\}\subset W_i.

(1) W_i is a regular noetherian scheme. Indeed C is smooth over the field k, hence regular, and is noetherian as a scheme of finite type over a field; W_i is an open subscheme of C, and both regularity and the noetherian property are preserved under passage to open subschemes.

(2) Z_i is a regular closed subscheme of W_i. Since the points p_1,\dots,p_m are distinct, p_{i+1}\notin\{p_1,\dots,p_i\}, so p_{i+1} is a point of W_i. Its closure in W_i is W_i\cap \overline{\{p_{i+1}\}}^{\,C}=\{p_{i+1}\} because p_{i+1} is a closed point of C; hence p_{i+1} is a closed point of the 1-dimensional noetherian scheme W_i, and Z_i is the corresponding closed subscheme with the reduced structure. The local ring O_{W_i,p_{i+1}} is the localization of the regular local ring O_{C,p_{i+1}} at the same prime ideal. Since C is a smooth (hence regular) curve, O_{C,p_{i+1}} is a regular local ring of dimension 1, i.e. a discrete valuation ring, and so is O_{W_i,p_{i+1}}. The ideal sheaf I_{Z_i} of Z_i in W_i is therefore locally principal, generated near p_{i+1} by a uniformizer \pi of O_{W_i,p_{i+1}}, which is a non-zero divisor (O_{W_i,p_{i+1}} is a domain, being a localization of the regular local ring O_{C,p_{i+1}}). Thus the closed immersion Z_i\hookrightarrow W_i is regular of codimension 1, and Z_i\cong\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(p_{i+1}) is a regular scheme (its unique local ring is the field \kappa(p_{i+1})). Also W_i\setminus Z_i = W_{i+1}.

(3) The residue field \kappa(p_{i+1}) is a finite field: p_{i+1} is a closed point of the curve C over the finite field k, so \kappa(p_{i+1}) is a finite extension of k.

(4) Apply the localization exact sequence, lemma_54 (eoinm/lemma_54), to the regular noetherian scheme U=W_i, the regular closed subscheme Z=Z_i, and V=W_{i+1}=W_i\setminus Z_i, with n>1. We obtain an exact sequence
K_n(Z_i)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to K_n(W_i)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{g_i} K_n(W_{i+1})\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to K_{n-1}(Z_i)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q.

(5) Vanishing of the two end terms. Since Z_i=\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(p_{i+1}), its K-groups are those of the field \kappa(p_{i+1}): K_r(Z_i)=K_r(\kappa(p_{i+1})) for every r\ge 0 (Quillen K-theory of the one-point scheme \mathrm{Spec}\,F is the K-theory of the ring F). By lemma_14 (eoinm/lemma_14) applied to the finite field \kappa(p_{i+1}), K_r(\kappa(p_{i+1}))\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0 for every r>0. In particular, taking r=n (which is >1, hence >0) and r=n-1 (which is \ge 1, hence >0, since n>1), we get
K_n(Z_i)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q = 0 \quad\text{and}\quad K_{n-1}(Z_i)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q = 0.
