(6) The sequence in (4) therefore reads 0 \to K_n(W_i)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{g_i} K_n(W_{i+1})\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to 0 and is exact at the two middle terms. Exactness at K_n(W_i)\otimes\mathbf Q gives \ker g_i = \mathrm{im}(K_n(Z_i)\otimes\mathbf Q \to K_n(W_i)\otimes\mathbf Q)=0, so g_i is injective. Exactness at K_n(W_{i+1})\otimes\mathbf Q gives \mathrm{im}\,g_i = \ker(K_n(W_{i+1})\otimes\mathbf Q \to K_{n-1}(Z_i)\otimes\mathbf Q)=K_n(W_{i+1})\otimes\mathbf Q (the last equality because the target is 0), so g_i is surjective. Hence g_i is an isomorphism of Q-vector spaces. This proves the claim.

Step 3 (composition). Compose the isomorphisms from the claim:
K_n(C)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q = K_n(W_0)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{g_0} K_n(W_1)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{g_1} \cdots \xrightarrow{g_{m-1}} K_n(W_m)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q = K_n(C\setminus S)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q.
Each g_i is the restriction map attached to the open immersion W_{i+1}\hookrightarrow W_i. By functoriality of Quillen K-theory with respect to composition of open immersions, the composite g_{m-1}\circ\cdots\circ g_1\circ g_0 : K_n(W_0)\to K_n(W_m) equals the restriction map attached to the composite open immersion C\setminus S = W_m \hookrightarrow W_0 = C; tensoring with the flat Z-module \mathbf Q commutes with taking this composite, so the displayed composite of the g_i is exactly j^*\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf Q} for j:C\setminus S\hookrightarrow C. A composition of isomorphisms is an isomorphism, so j^*\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf Q}: K_n(C)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to K_n(C\setminus S)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q is an isomorphism of Q-vector spaces. Together with Step 1 this completes the proof.

lemma_87.statement: Let k be a finite field and let X be a smooth projective variety over k of dimension at least 1. Then there exists a finite separable extension k'/k such that X_{k'} has a nonempty smooth hyperplane section for some projective embedding over k'.
lemma_87.proof:
Let d = dim X >= 1. Let K be an algebraic closure of k. Since k is a finite field, every finite extension of k is separable; it suffices to find a finite extension k'/k.

1. Choose a very ample line bundle L on X. This exists because X is projective. Put V = H^0(X,L), a finite dimensional k-vector space. The complete linear system of L gives a closed immersion i: X -> P(V^*)_k. For any field extension F/k, base change gives a very ample line bundle L_F on X_F and a closed immersion i_F: X_F -> P(V_F^*)_F, where V_F = H^0(X_F,L_F) = V tensor_k F (cohomology and base change for projective morphisms).

2. Over K, set X_K = X times_k K. We prove that there is a nonzero section s of L_K whose zero scheme Y = V(s) is nonempty and smooth over K.

Let J^1(L_K) be the first jet bundle of L_K. Its fiber at a point x is the space of first jets of sections of L_K at x; since X_K is smooth of dimension d, this fiber has dimension d+1. For a section s and a point x, j^1_x(s)=0 iff s(x)=0 and the differential of s at x is zero.

The evaluation map ev_1: V_K tensor O_{X_K} -> J^1(L_K), sending a constant section of the trivial bundle to its first jet, is fiberwise surjective. Indeed, L_K is very ample, so i_K is a closed immersion. At a point x choose a section s_0 with s_0(x) not equal to 0. In the local trivialization by s_0, the remaining sections give local functions f_1,...,f_N whose values and differentials at x are the local coordinates of i_K near x. The value part gives the whole fiber L_K,x, and because i_K is an immersion the differentials df_1,...,df_N span the cotangent space (L_K,x) tensor Omega^1_{X_K/K,x}. Hence every first jet at x is obtained. Thus ev_1 is a surjection of vector bundles. Let E be its kernel; E is a vector bundle of rank r = dim V_K - (d+1).

Consider the subset Z = { (x, [s]) in X_K times P(V_K) : j^1_x(s)=0 } of X_K times P(V_K). The condition is homogeneous in s and is given by linear equations in the coordinates of s, so Z is closed. Its fiber over x is the projective space of lines in E_x, so Z is a projective bundle over X_K (empty if r=0) of relative dimension r-1 = dim V_K - d - 2. Therefore dim Z = d + dim V_K - d - 2 = dim V_K - 2 (with the convention that Z is empty when r=0). Let pi: Z -> P(V_K) be the second projection. Since Z is closed in the product of two projective K-varieties, pi is proper, and B = pi(Z) is a closed subset of P(V_K). By construction, B is exactly the set of sections [s] for which the zero scheme V(s) has a point at which the first jet vanishes, i.e. a singular point.

The ambient projective space P(V_K) has dimension dim V_K - 1. Hence dim B is at most dim Z = dim V_K - 2, so B is a proper closed subset. Choose [s] in the nonempty open complement U = P(V_K) minus B.

For this s, no point of X_K has j^1_x(s)=0. We show Y=V(s) is nonempty and smooth. If Y were empty, s would be nowhere vanishing and would trivialize L_K. But L_K is very ample, hence ample, and the trivial line bundle is not very ample on a positive-dimensional projective scheme: its complete linear system is given by global regular functions, which are constant on each connected component, so the associated morphism is constant on positive-dimensional components and cannot be a closed immersion. Thus Y is nonempty. Now take any y in Y. In a local trivialization of L_K near y, s corresponds to a regular function f with f(y)=0. The condition j^1_y(s) not equal to 0 means df_y not equal to 0. Since O_{X_K,y} is a regular local ring of dimension d, an element of the maximal ideal whose differential is nonzero is part of a regular system of parameters. Consequently O_{X_K,y}/(f) is a regular local ring of dimension d-1. By the hypersurface criterion (the Jacobian criterion), Y is smooth over K at y. Since y was arbitrary, Y is a nonempty smooth K-scheme of dimension d-1.

3. Descent to a finite extension. Write s as a K-linear combination of a k-basis of V: s = a_1 e_1 + ... + a_m e_m with a_i in K. Let k' be the finite subextension of K generated by the a_i. Since k is a finite field, k'/k is finite and separable. Then s lies in V_{k'} = H^0(X_{k'}, L_{k'}). Let H be the hyperplane in P(V_{k'}^*) corresponding to s, and let Y' = X_{k'} intersect H. By construction, the base change of Y' to K is exactly Y.

Smoothness descends under faithfully flat base change: K/k' is a field extension, hence faithfully flat, and (Y')_K = Y is smooth over K; therefore Y' is smooth over k'. If Y' were empty, its base change to K would be empty, contradicting that Y is nonempty. Hence Y' is nonempty.

The morphism i_{k'}: X_{k'} -> P(V_{k'}^*)_{k'} is a projective embedding, and Y' is the hyperplane section cut out by H. This gives the required finite separable extension k'/k and required smooth nonempty hyperplane section.

lemma_89.statement: Let k be a finite field, let k'/k be a finite separable extension, let X be a regular noetherian scheme over k, and let n > 0. Then the homomorphism K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \to K_n(X_{k'}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} induced by the base change X \mapsto X_{k'} is injective.
lemma_89.proof: Let d = [k':k] and let f: X_{k'} → X be the projection. We prove that f^* is injective. Step 1. f is finite locally free of rank d and X_{k'} is regular noetherian. Since k' is a finite free k-module of rank d, Spec k' → Spec k is finite locally free of rank d; base change by X gives a finite locally free morphism f of rank d. Because k'/k is finite separable, Spec k' → Spec k is finite étale, hence f is finite étale. The scheme X_{k'} is noetherian because f is finite and X is noetherian. To see regularity, take an affine open U = Spec A of X and a point y of f^{-1}(U) = Spec B with B = A ⊗_k k', and let p ⊂ A and q ⊂ B be the corresponding primes. Let m_p and m_q be the maximal ideals of A_p and B_q. Then B_q is finite étale over A_p. Since B_q is finite over A_p, dim B_q = dim A_p. The quotient B_q / m_p B_q is a finite étale algebra over the field A_p / m_p, hence a product of finite separable field extensions; because B_q is local, this quotient is local, so it is a field and its maximal ideal is zero. Therefore m_q = m_p B_q. The ring A_p is regular, so m_p is generated by dim A_p elements. Their images generate m_p B_q = m_q, so m_q is generated by dim A_p = dim B_q elements. Thus B_q is a regular local ring. Since y was arbitrary, X_{k'} is regular. Step 2. The pushforward f_* O_{X_{k'}} is isomorphic to O_X^{⊕ d}. Choose a k-basis e_1, ..., e_d of k'. For every affine open U = Spec A ⊂ X, the restriction of f_* O_{X_{k'}} to U is A ⊗_k k', and the map A^{⊕ d} → A ⊗_k k', (a_i) ↦ Σ a_i ⊗ e_i, is an isomorphism of A-modules. These isomorphisms are compatible on overlaps because they use the same basis, so they glue to a global sheaf isomorphism f_* O_{X_{k'}} ≅ O_X^{⊕ d}. Consequently, in K_0(X), [f_* O_{X_{k'}}] = [O_X^{⊕ d}] = d [O_X]. Step 3. Apply the proved lemma with user_id eoinm and lemma_id lemma_58 to the finite locally free morphism f: X_{k'} → X of rank d. The hypotheses are satisfied: X and X_{k'} are regular noetherian, d ≥ 1, n > 0, and the class condition from Step 2 holds. Hence the composite f_* ∘ f^*: K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q → K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q is multiplication by d. Step 4. Let x ∈ K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q with f^*(x) = 0. Then d x = (f_* ∘ f^*)(x) = f_*(0) = 0. Since K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q is a Q-vector space and d is a positive integer, multiplication by d is injective; thus x = 0. Therefore f^* is injective.

lemma_90.statement: Let k be a finite field, let k'/k be a finite separable extension, let X be a regular noetherian scheme over k, and let n > 0. If K_n(X_{k'}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0, then K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.
lemma_90.proof:
Let k be a finite field, let k'/k be a finite separable extension, let X be a regular noetherian scheme over k, and let n > 0. Assume K_n(X_{k'}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0. We must show K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.

Step 1 (the base change map). Let \varphi: K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \to K_n(X_{k'}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} denote the homomorphism of \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces induced by the base change morphism X_{k'} = X \times_k k' \to X (i.e., \varphi is the map on K-theory with rational coefficients induced by the structural morphism X \to \mathrm{Spec}\,k followed by the inclusion \mathrm{Spec}\,k \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Spec}\,k', equivalently the pullback along X_{k'} \to X). Since tensoring with \mathbf{Q} is exact, both K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} and K_n(X_{k'}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} are \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces and \varphi is \mathbf{Q}-linear.

Step 2 (injectivity, via lemma_89). The hypotheses of the proved lemma (user_id "eoinm", lemma_id "lemma_89") are: k a finite field, k'/k a finite separable extension, X a regular noetherian scheme over k, and n > 0. These are precisely the hypotheses of the present statement, so lemma_89 applies and yields that \varphi is injective, i.e., \ker \varphi = \{0\}.

Step 3 (conclusion). Let v \in K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} be arbitrary. Its image \varphi(v) lies in the codomain K_n(X_{k'}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q}, which is the zero vector space by hypothesis. Hence \varphi(v) = 0. Since \varphi is injective by Step 2, v \in \ker \varphi = \{0\}, so v = 0. As v was arbitrary, every element of K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} is zero, i.e., K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.

This completes the proof.

lemma_91.statement: Let k be a finite field and let F/k be a finitely generated field extension of transcendence degree 1. Let k_0 be the algebraic closure of k in F. Then there exists a smooth projective geometrically integral curve C over k_0 whose function field is F.
lemma_91.proof:
We prove the assertion in four steps.

Step 1. k_0 is a finite field. Let S={x_1,...,x_m} be a finite set of generators of F over k. Choose u\in F transcendental over k; such an element exists because trdeg_k F=1. Since k_0/k is algebraic, u is transcendental over k_0: if u were algebraic over k_0, it would be algebraic over k. Hence trdeg_{k_0} F=1 and F is algebraic over k_0(u).

First, F is finite over k(u). Indeed F=k(S) is generated over k(u) by the finite set S, and F is algebraic over k(u) because F is algebraic over k_0(u) and k_0(u) is algebraic over k(u). A field extension that is algebraic and finitely generated as a field extension is finite (Zariski's lemma), so [F:k(u)] is finite.

Second, F is finite over k_0(u). We have F=k_0(S), because k_0\subset F and S\subset F imply k_0(S)\subset F, while F=k(S)\subset k_0(S). This is algebraic and finitely generated over k_0(u), hence finite.

Now k(u)\subset k_0(u)\subset F. By the tower law for field degrees, [k_0(u):k(u)] is finite. If {e_i} is a k-basis of k_0 (possibly infinite), then the e_i are k(u)-linearly independent: a relation \sum_i e_i f_i(u)=0 with f_i(u)\in k(u) can be cleared of denominators to a relation \sum_i e_i g_i(u)=0 with g_i(u)\in k[u], and comparing coefficients forces every g_i(u)=0. Therefore [k_0(u):k(u)]\ge [k_0:k]. Since the left-hand side is finite, [k_0:k] is finite. As k is finite, k_0 is a finite field.

Step 2. Choose a separating variable. The field k_0 is finite, hence perfect. Since k_0/k is finite and F/k is finitely generated, F/k_0 is finitely generated. By construction k_0 is algebraically closed in F: if x\in F is algebraic over k_0, then x is algebraic over k, so x\in k_0. Since k_0 is perfect, every finitely generated extension of k_0 is separably generated (standard field-theoretic fact); as F/k_0 is finitely generated and k_0 is algebraically closed in F, F/k_0 is a regular extension. Hence there exists a separating transcendence basis; because trdeg_{k_0} F=1, it consists of one element t\in F, transcendental over k_0, such that F/k_0(t) is finite separable.

Step 3. An affine smooth model. Let R=k_0[t]. This is a principal ideal domain, hence a Dedekind domain. Let A be the integral closure of R in F. Because F/k_0(t) is finite separable, the standard integral closure theorem for Dedekind domains says that A is a finite R-module and is a Dedekind domain. Its fraction field is F.

Since A is finite over R, it is a finitely generated k_0-algebra: if a_1,...,a_s is a set of R-module generators of A, then A=k_0[t,a_1,...,a_s]. As a one-dimensional Noetherian integrally closed domain, A is regular. A regular scheme of finite type over a perfect field is smooth, so X=Spec A is a smooth affine curve over k_0 with function field F.

Moreover X is geometrically integral. We use the standard criterion: if B is a k_0-domain of finite type with fraction field L, then B is geometrically integral over k_0 whenever L/k_0 is regular. For completeness, if L/k_0 is regular then L\otimes_{k_0} k_0' is a domain for every field extension k_0'/k_0; since B\subset L and k_0' is flat over k_0, the map B\otimes_{k_0} k_0'\to L\otimes_{k_0} k_0' is injective, so B\otimes_{k_0} k_0' is a domain. Here B=A and L=F, and F/k_0 is regular as shown in Step 2.

Step 4. Projective smooth completion. Embed X as a closed subscheme of affine space \mathbf{A}^N_{k_0} using the finite generators of A. Let Y be the projective closure of X in \mathbf{P}^N_{k_0}. Then Y is an integral projective curve over k_0, X is a nonempty dense open subscheme of Y, and the function field of Y is F.

Let C be the normalization of Y in its function field F. For a projective integral curve, the normalization is finite and projective. Hence C is an integral projective curve over k_0 with function field F. Since C is normal and one-dimensional, it is regular; over the perfect field k_0 this implies C is smooth. Finally, C is a k_0-domain of finite type whose fraction field is F, and F/k_0 is regular; by the same criterion as in Step 3, C is geometrically integral.

Thus C is a smooth projective geometrically integral curve over k_0 whose function field is F.

lemma_94_milnor_K2_finite_field.statement: Let k be a finite field, and let K_2^M(k) be the abelian group generated by symbols {a,b} with a,b in k^*, subject to the relations {a,bc} = {a,b} + {a,c}, {ab,c} = {a,c} + {b,c}, and {a,1-a} = 0 for a in k^*, a \neq 1. Then K_2^M(k) = 0.
lemma_94_milnor_K2_finite_field.proof:
Let G=K_2^M(k) be the abelian group in the statement, written additively. Put q=|k| and n=q-1.

Step 1. Symbols with a 1 are zero. For any a,c in k^*, the relation {a,bc}={a,b}+{a,c} with b=1 gives {a,c}={a,1}+{a,c}; adding the inverse of {a,c} yields {a,1}=0. Similarly, the relation {ab,c}={a,c}+{b,c} with a=1 gives {b,c}={1,c}+{b,c}; hence {1,c}=0.

Step 2. The case q=2. Then k^*={1}, so the only generator is {1,1}. By Step 1, {1,1}=0, and G=0.

Step 3. The case q>2. Let H=k^*. We first show H is cyclic. Let e be the exponent of H, the least common multiple of the orders of all its elements. Every element of H satisfies x^e=1, so the polynomial T^e-1 over k has all n elements of H as roots; a nonzero polynomial of degree e over a field has at most e roots, hence n<=e. Also e divides n, because every element order divides n and the lcm of divisors of n divides n. Thus e=n. For each prime p dividing e, by definition of e there is some element of H whose order is divisible by p^{v_p(e)}; raising that element to the power obtained by removing the p-part gives an element h_p of order p^{v_p(e)}. The h_p commute and have pairwise coprime orders. Their product h has order e. Since each h_p has order dividing e, h^e=1, so the order m of h divides e. Let E_p=e/p^{v_p(e)}. If h^m=1, then h^{mE_p}=1. For q different from p, the order of h_q divides E_p, so h_q^{mE_p}=1; hence h_p^{mE_p}=1. Because E_p is coprime to p^{v_p(e)}, p^{v_p(e)} divides m. This holds for every p, so e divides m. Thus m=e. Therefore h has order n and generates H. Choose such a generator g.

Let x={g,g}. We claim that for all positive integers i,j, {g^i,g^j}=ij x. First, by induction on i using {ab,c}={a,c}+{b,c}, {g^i,g}=i x: the case i=1 is x, and {g^{i+1},g}={g^i g,g}={g^i,g}+{g,g}. Second, for fixed a and by induction on j using {a,bc}={a,b}+{a,c}, {a,g^j}=j{a,g}: the case j=1 is {a,g}, and {a,g^{j+1}}={a,g^j g}={a,g^j}+{a,g}. Taking a=g^i gives {g^i,g^j}=j{g^i,g}=j(i x)=ij x.

Since g^n=1, Step 1 gives {g^n,g}={1,g}=0. The formula with i=n,j=1 gives n x=0.

For each i=1,...,n-1, g^i is not 1. The element 1-g^i is nonzero, and it is not 1 because 1-g^i=1 would imply g^i=0. Hence 1-g^i lies in H and can be written uniquely as g^{k_i} with k_i in {1,...,n-1}. The Steinberg relation with a=g^i gives {g^i,1-g^i}=0, i.e. {g^i,g^{k_i}}=0. By the power formula, i k_i x=0 for every i=1,...,n-1.

The map i->k_i is a permutation of {1,...,n-1}. Indeed, the map t->1-t from H minus {1} to H minus {1} is bijective, with inverse itself; as t runs through the n-1 elements g^i (i=1,...,n-1), 1-t runs through the n-1 elements g^{k_i} in the same way.

Let D be the gcd of the integers n, k_1, 2k_2, ..., (n-1)k_{n-1}. The relations n x=0 and i k_i x=0 show that D x=0. We prove D=1. Suppose a prime ell divides D. Then ell divides n. For every i in {1,...,n-1} with ell not dividing i, we have ell | i k_i, hence ell | k_i. The number of such i is n - n/ell. Since i->k_i is a permutation, the corresponding k_i are distinct multiples of ell in {1,...,n-1}. The number of positive multiples of ell not exceeding n-1 is n/ell - 1. Therefore n - n/ell <= n/ell - 1, which is equivalent to ell(n+1) <= 2n. This is impossible for ell>=2, since ell(n+1) >= 2n+2. Thus no prime divides D, so D=1.

By Bezout's identity, there are integers u, v_1,...,v_{n-1} such that u n + v_1 k_1 + v_2 (2k_2)+...+v_{n-1}((n-1)k_{n-1})=1. Multiplying x by this identity and using n x=0 and i k_i x=0 for each i gives x=0.

Finally, take arbitrary a,b in H. Write a=g^i and b=g^j with i,j in {0,...,n-1}. If i=0 or j=0, then a=1 or b=1, and Step 1 gives {a,b}=0. If 1<=i,j<=n-1, the power formula gives {a,b}=ij x=0. Thus every generator of G is zero, so G=0. This completes the proof.

lemma_88_only_if.statement: Let k be a finite field and let Z be a smooth affine scheme of dimension at most 2 over k. If K_1(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0, then \mathcal{O}_Z^* is torsion.
lemma_88_only_if.proof: Let R = Gamma(Z, O_Z). Since Z is affine, we use the standard identification K_1(Z) = K_1(R) = GL_infty(R)/E_infty(R), where GL_infty(R) is the direct limit of GL_m(R) under A -> diag(A,1) and E_infty(R) is generated by elementary matrices. The determinant gives a homomorphism det: K_1(R) -> R^*, defined by det([A]) = det(A) for A in GL_m(R). It is well-defined because elementary matrices have determinant 1 and adding an identity block does not change the determinant. It is a homomorphism because det(AB) = det(A)det(B). The map i: R^* -> K_1(R), i(u) = [(u)] (the class of the 1x1 invertible matrix u), is a homomorphism and det(i(u)) = u. Hence det is surjective, so R^* is a quotient of K_1(R). Let A = K_1(R), B = R^*, and q = det. The hypothesis is A tensor_Z Q = 0. For any element b tensor r of B tensor_Z Q, choose a in A with q(a) = b. Then b tensor r = q(a) tensor r = (q tensor id_Q)(a tensor r) = 0, since a tensor r lies in A tensor_Z Q = 0. Therefore B tensor_Z Q = 0. We now show that B tensor_Z Q = 0 implies B is torsion. Let S be the set of nonzero integers; Q is the localization of Z at S, so B tensor_Z Q is canonically isomorphic to the localization of B at S, denoted B_S. Under this isomorphism, b tensor 1 corresponds to b/1. In a localization, b/1 = 0 if and only if there exists s in S with s b = 0: if b/1 = 0/1, then some t in S satisfies t b = 0; conversely, if s b = 0, then b/1 = 0/s. Since B_S = 0, b/1 = 0 for every b in B, so every b is annihilated by some nonzero integer. Thus B is torsion. Applying this to B = R^* = O_Z^* proves that O_Z^* is torsion. The assumptions that k is finite and that dim Z <= 2 are not needed for this direction; the argument works for any affine scheme.

lemma_97_milnor_K2_tame_symbol.statement: Let k be a finite field, let F=k((t)) with t-adic valuation v, and let K_2^M(F) be the abelian group generated by symbols {a,b} (a,b in F^*) subject to {ab,c}={a,c}+{b,c}, {a,bc}={a,b}+{a,c}, and {a,1-a}=0. For a,b in F^* write a=t^{v(a)}u_a and b=t^{v(b)}u_b with u_a,u_b in k[[t]]^*, and set ts({a,b})=(-1)^{v(a)v(b)} (u_a mod t)^{v(b)} (u_b mod t)^{-v(a)} in k^*, where (-1)^m is 1 if m is even and -1 if m is odd. Then ts is a surjective group homomorphism K_2^M(F) -> k^*.
lemma_97_milnor_K2_tame_symbol.proof: Let F^* be the multiplicative group of F. For z in F^* write z=t^{m_z}u_z with m_z=v(z) and u_z in k[[t]]^*, and set z_0 = u_z mod t in k^*. Define f: F^* x F^* -> k^* by f(x,y)=(-1)^{m_x m_y} x_0^{m_y} y_0^{-m_x}; powers with negative exponents are interpreted in the abelian group k^*. We first check the two bilinearity relations. For x,y,z in F^*, m_{xy}=m_x+m_y and (xy)_0=x_0 y_0 because the t-adic valuation is additive and reduction modulo t is a ring homomorphism k[[t]]^* -> k^*. Hence f(xy,z)=(-1)^{(m_x+m_y)m_z} (x_0 y_0)^{m_z} z_0^{-(m_x+m_y)} = (-1)^{m_x m_z}(-1)^{m_y m_z} x_0^{m_z} y_0^{m_z} z_0^{-m_x} z_0^{-m_y} = f(x,z) f(y,z). Similarly f(x,yz)=(-1)^{m_x(m_y+m_z)} x_0^{m_y+m_z} (y_0 z_0)^{-m_x} = (-1)^{m_x m_y}(-1)^{m_x m_z} x_0^{m_y} x_0^{m_z} y_0^{-m_x} z_0^{-m_x} = f(x,y) f(x,z). Now check the relation {a,1-a}=0. Let a in F^*, a != 1, and put y=1-a. If m_a>0, then y is a unit with y_0=1, so f(a,y)=(-1)^{m_a 0} a_0^0 1^{-m_a}=1. If m_a<0, write m=-m_a>0 and a=t^{-m}u with u_0=c in k^*. Then y=1-a=t^{-m}(t^m-u). The element t^m-u is a unit: its residue is -c, which is nonzero. Thus m_y=-m and y_0=-c. Therefore f(a,y)=(-1)^{(-m)(-m)} c^{-m} (-c)^m = (-1)^{m^2} (-1)^m = (-1)^{m^2+m}=1, since m^2+m=m(m+1) is even. If m_a=0, write a=u with u_0=c. If c=1, then u-1 has positive valuation, hence y=1-a has positive valuation, and f(a,y)=(-1)^0 c^{m_y} y_0^0=1. If c != 1, then y_0=1-c != 0, so m_y=0, and f(a,y)=(-1)^0 c^0 y_0^0=1. Thus f vanishes on all defining relations of K_2^M(F). Since K_2^M(F) is the quotient of the free abelian group on F^* x F^* by the subgroup generated by (xy,z)-(x,z)-(y,z), (x,yz)-(x,y)-(x,z), and (a,1-a), the checks above induce a unique group homomorphism ts: K_2^M(F) -> k^* with ts({x,y})=f(x,y). For surjectivity, let c in k^*. Take x=c (viewed as a constant element of F^*) and y=t. Then m_x=0, x_0=c, m_y=1, y_0=1, so ts({c,t})=f(c,t)=(-1)^0 c^1 1^0=c. Hence the image of ts contains every element of k^*, so ts is surjective. This completes the proof.
